long thin stone blades
Long blades struck one by one from a prepared core are the mark of the Upper Palaeolithic: one stone yields many times more cutting edge.
the bow and arrow
Stone arrowheads from Grotte Mandrin, France (about 54,000 years) and a Sri Lankan cave (about 48,000) are among the oldest bow evidence known outside Africa.
the eyed bone needle
Needles made close-fitting clothes possible, and with them survival in Ice Age cold. Some of the oldest eyed bone needles are about 40,000 years old or more.
nets and barbed bone harpoons
Barbed bone harpoons made big fish catchable, turning rivers and coasts into key food sources.
the spear-thrower
A spear-thrower hurls a dart far harder and farther than an arm alone. The clearest evidence comes from France, about 17,000–20,000 years ago.
the stone fat lamp
Stone lamps burning animal fat carried light deep into caves; several have been found at Lascaux.
flint-bladed sickles
Flint blades used again and again on grasses take on a glossy sheen; archaeologists find it on Natufian sickles over 12,000 years old.
grinding stones
Grinding stones turn hard seed into flour and porridge that babies can eat, so mothers could wean earlier and have children closer together.
fired clay pots

Pottery in East Asia is far older than farming: sherds from Xianrendong cave in China are about 20,000 years old. Saharan peoples made their own pots from about 10,000 years ago, and in the Near East pottery spread around 8,500 years ago.
mud brick
Sun-dried mud brick built Jericho, and Çatalhöyük, where houses packed so tightly that people entered through the roofs.
woven linen
Linen from Nahal Hemar cave in the Judean desert, about 9,000 years old, is among the oldest woven cloth in the Near East.
the star compass
Wayfinders memorise where dozens of stars rise and set around the horizon, and use them as a compass.
reading ocean swells
Wayfinders feel several long swells from different directions through the hull, and know how islands bend them.
following seabirds
Some seabirds feed not far from land and fly home at dusk, so the way they fly shows where land lies.
reading clouds over islands
Clouds tend to sit still over islands, and atoll lagoons cast a green tint onto their undersides.
the double-hulled voyaging canoe
A double-hulled canoe carries enough people, food, pigs, dogs, chickens and plant cuttings to settle a new island.
the crab-claw sail
The crab-claw sail is an Austronesian design that sails well across the wind.

Natufians hunted gazelle as a staple for thousands of years, but no one ever domesticated it: it panics, leaps high, and will not live as a herd under people. Most wild animals cannot be domesticated for reasons like these.
Most deer are territorial and skittish, and the males turn violent in the rut. Of all the deer, only reindeer were ever herded, and much later.
At Uan Afuda cave in Libya, about 9,000 years ago, people seem to have penned wild Barbary sheep inside the cave, leaving thick layers of dung, yet Barbary sheep never became truly domestic.

Domestic chickens descend from Southeast Asian junglefowl. Evidence from Ban Non Wat in Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand, shows domestic chickens by about 3,500 years ago, thousands of years after your time, and they may first have been kept for social reasons rather than food.
In New Guinea, cassowary eggshells about 18,000–6,000 years old suggest people collected eggs near hatching to raise the chicks. Grown cassowaries are very dangerous and were never herded.
Wild boar can be tamed, but domestic pigs reached mainland Southeast Asia with farmers from the north thousands of years later.

Turning a wild animal into a domestic one took centuries to millennia, as the tamest were bred generation after generation; the game squeezes this into one life. Goats from Ganj Dareh, Iran, about 10,000 years ago, are among the clearest early domestic goats.

Domestic sheep descend from wild mouflon of Anatolia and the Zagros; it took many generations, which the game squeezes into one life. Early sheep had no woolly fleece for weaving; that came thousands of years later.
Aurochs bulls stood nearly two metres tall and were ferocious. DNA studies suggest Near Eastern cattle may descend from only about 80 aurochs cows. The game squeezes many generations into one life.
Pigs were domesticated at least twice, in Anatolia and in China. They eat almost anything, including human scraps, which suits village life. The game squeezes many generations into one life.

There are hundreds of large animal species, but only a few dozen ever became truly domestic. The ones that did tend to eat many plants, grow fast, breed in pens, stay calm, and live in herds with a leader.

In early farming villages like Çatalhöyük nearly every house looks alike, and archaeologists see little inequality. But once animals, grain stores and land could pile up and be inherited, gaps between families began to form.
Many human diseases began in animals. Living close to herds, and crowded into villages, made it easier for germs to jump to people.
The Natufians of the Levant built permanent hamlets and harvested wild grasses before farming. At Ain Mallaha a woman was buried with a puppy about 12,000 years ago.
Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Anatolia has huge carved stone pillars about 11,600 years old, raised by people who still hunted and gathered.
Some of the clearest early domestic goats come from Ganj Dareh in the Zagros, about 10,000 years ago.
Millet was grown in north China from about 10,000 years ago; domestic pigs and crane-bone flutes at Jiahu are about 9,000 years old.
The Yangtze is where rice farming began. Shangshan shows rice use about 10,000 years ago, but fully domestic rice took thousands of years more.

From about 11,000 to 5,000 years ago the Sahara was far wetter, with lakes, hippos and crocodiles. People fished with bone harpoons and made their own pottery from about 10,000 years ago, and later began herding cattle.

Spirit Cave in Pang Mapha, excavated in the 1960s, holds traces of Hoabinhian people about 12,000–7,500 years ago. Its plant remains were once read as early farming; most scholars now see them as gathered wild plants.
Kuk Swamp in Papua New Guinea shows drainage ditches for gardens from about 10,000–7,000 years ago, one of the places farming began independently, with bananas grown by about 7,000 years ago.

Within a few thousand years, villages like yours will grow into towns. To the south, in Mesopotamia, farmers’ descendants will build the first cities and write the first script; some scholars think writing began with clay tokens for counting sheep and goats. Another line of your descendants will carry wheat and goats into Europe.
The millet and rice of your rivers will one day feed billions. Farmers from here will move south, carrying rice and pigs into Southeast Asia, including today’s Thailand, about 4,000 years ago.

About 5,000 years ago the rains fail and the Green Sahara turns to desert. People drive their cattle to the Nile and to the south; some think Saharan herders were among the roots of Egyptian civilisation.
Farmers from the north will arrive thousands of years later with rice, pigs and dogs. Descendants of foragers like you will mix with them, and the DNA of Southeast Asians today carries both lines.

New Guinea highlanders have gardened their valleys for nearly ten thousand years, to this day, yet the island had no large animal that could be herded; pigs arrived thousands of years later. Geography limited the choices, not the people.
For years the rain grows scarce and the winters long. The elders say they have never seen the like.

About 8,200 years ago a vast flood of meltwater from a North American ice lake entered the ocean, cooling and drying the world for nearly two centuries; some Near Eastern villages were abandoned or changed their ways.

Early farmers’ skeletons at many sites are shorter and have more tooth decay than foragers’, yet their numbers grew fast, because settled life meant more children. No one could see where this choice led within one lifetime.

In many later herding societies, lending animals binds families together: the borrower owes a debt of gratitude and helps when you are in trouble. Whether the first villagers did this is unknown; this part is a simulation.

Giving animals to the other family at marriage is found in many later herding societies, for example in East Africa. Whether the first villagers did so is unknown; this part is a simulation.

The harvest went well and people from other villages are coming. You have enough animals for a feast everyone will remember.
Göbekli Tepe holds enormous quantities of animal bone; many archaeologists think great feasts were how many groups were brought together to work.
Feasts where a host gives away great amounts of food are a way of building prestige and social ties found in many societies worldwide.
Held a feast everyone remembered
The fires blaze all night; strangers sing songs you have never heard. They will remember your name.

Once animals and land could be inherited, wealth began to build up across generations, and dividing an inheritance became a source of family quarrels that lasts to this day.

Your herd grows, but the house is quieter.

Everyone is surprised, and no one forgets.

Cats probably domesticated themselves, drawn to the mice that ate village grain. At Shillourokambos on Cyprus, about 9,500 years ago, a cat was buried near a person; cats are not native to Cyprus, so people must have carried them across the sea.

Within months the mice are gone, and the cat sleeps by the hearth.

It vanishes into the dark, and the mice return.

Dogs were bred from wolves thousands of years before farming. At Ain Mallaha in the Levant, about 12,000 years ago, a woman was buried with her hand resting on a puppy. Dogs guard herds from wolves.

It follows another child instead.

Milk fats in pots from northwest Anatolia are about 8,500 years old. Almost no adults then could digest milk sugar; souring it or making cheese reduces that sugar. Adult milk digestion spread thousands of years later.

Too late; it is already through the herd.

The meat is not wasted.

Several die, but the rite lets everyone feel they did all they could.

Everyone fears the store-keepers will cheat.

People from many groups gather on a hilltop to cut huge limestone pillars and carve animals on them.

Göbekli Tepe was raised about 11,600 years ago by people who still hunted and gathered. Some pillars stand over 5 metres, carved with foxes, boars, snakes and vultures. It led some archaeologists to ask whether shared ritual came before farming rather than after.
Help haul the stone
A hundred people pull together, and the pillar slowly rises. You feel part of something bigger than your band.

Carved an animal on a Göbekli Tepe pillar
Ten thousand years later someone will stand before this fox and wonder who carved it.
Lead the rite on the hill
Every band falls silent when you begin to sing.
You chase a kid goat until you tumble in the dust; the grown-ups roar with laughter.
The whole village helps re-plaster the house floors before the rains.
At harvest everyone sleeps in the fields to keep birds and boar away.
A stranger from another valley brings seeds you have never seen, to trade.
The first Near Eastern crops, such as wheat, barley, lentils and flax, were brought into cultivation in several places and traded between valleys; not every village had to invent them.
You paddle a dugout onto the lake and spear fish with a bone harpoon.
A group of herders drive their cattle to the lake. You have never seen cattle that follow people.
Whether cattle herding in North Africa came from the Near East or also began locally is still debated. Saharan rock art is full of cattle.
You gather areca nuts, beans and gourds from the forest and carry them up to the cave.
Plant remains from Spirit Cave, such as areca, beans and gourds, were once read as early farming, but most scholars later saw them as gathered from the wild.
You strike river pebbles into one-sided tools, as everyone in your band does.
Pebble tools flaked on one face are the hallmark of the Hoabinhian, found across Southeast Asia, including many caves in northern and western Thailand.
Everyone digs drainage ditches in the swamp, so the soil is dry enough for taro.
An elder plays a flute made from a crane’s wing bone; its sound carries across the village.
Crane-bone flutes from Jiahu, China, about 9,000 years old, can still be played today.
Everyone works to raise the village’s great stone wall and tower.
The stone tower of Jericho, about 10,000 years old and some 8 metres tall, is one of the oldest large structures. Whether it was for floods, enemies or ritual is still debated.

At Jericho and Tell Aswad, about 10,000–9,000 years ago, people buried the dead under house floors, then lifted the skulls and modelled faces on them in plaster, with shells for eyes. At Ain Mallaha a woman was buried with a puppy.
At Çatalhöyük the dead were buried beneath the sleeping platforms inside houses, so the living slept above their ancestors every night. Some were dusted with red ochre.
Graves at Jiahu, China, about 9,000 years ago, sometimes held crane-bone flutes and turtle shells filled with pebbles.
At Gobero in Niger, people buried their dead beside an ancient lake that is desert today, some with ornaments.
At many Hoabinhian sites the dead were buried curled up, sometimes with red ochre or stone tools.
There is no clear evidence of how New Guinea highlanders of this time treated their dead; this is a simulation.

No one will play that flute again.

The red looks warm against the cold earth.
You are buried beneath the house floor. A year later your descendants lift your skull, give it a plaster face with shell eyes, and set it in the house.
You are buried beneath the floor where you slept. Your family goes on living above you every day.
The band buries you curled as if asleep, under red ochre.
The sea swallows the land
The shore where the elders camped as children is under water now, and every year the sea creeps closer.

As the ice melted the sea rose over 100 metres; about 14,500 years ago it rose especially fast, some 15–20 metres in a few centuries. Nearly half of Sundaland, which joined the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java and Borneo, went under. The coastal camps of its people now lie beneath the sea, and we know almost nothing of them.
Move upriver to higher ground
The upland forest is strange, but the ground stays under your feet.
Stay and fish the new shallows
Fish crowd the drowned mangroves, but every storm pushes the water deeper.
Tell the children of the land that sank
The children ask when the sea will stop. You cannot say, but your story will outlast the shore.
The village under the sea
The elders say a great village of the ancestors lies beneath the sea, with houses of stone and fires that never die. One night, at an unusually low tide, you see a faint light far out over the water.

This is made up. Some have claimed Sundaland held an advanced civilisation that sank, but no archaeology supports it; what really drowned were coasts where foragers and fishers lived. Many Southeast Asian peoples have great-flood myths, which some think may remember the rising sea, though that cannot be proven.

The water is icy, and the light is gone when you come near, but in your hand is a green stone bead you cannot explain.

A wide grassland stretches east until the far forest is out of sight; herds of banteng graze in the distance.

During glacial times the climate was drier than today. Some researchers propose a corridor of grassland through the heart of Sundaland, a highway for people and animals rather like the African savanna, though this is debated and it may have been open woodland mixed with grass.
A great herd of elephants crosses the river, the calves holding their mothers’ tails.
The Sunda plains now under the sea were home to elephants, rhinos, tapirs, tigers, banteng, wild water buffalo, and orangutans living much farther south than today.

At Niah Cave in Borneo, evidence from about 50,000–40,000 years ago shows people managing rainforest with fire and knowing how to remove toxins from certain plants before eating them, a remarkably sophisticated knowledge.
A tiger circles the camp all night. No one dares to sleep.

The first thing you made
You shape riverside clay into a little cup and sneak it beside the fire until it hardens.
You set tiny flint flakes in a row along a grooved bone handle, and have your very own first sickle.
You pick a flat pebble from the stream and flake one face until it can cut bamboo.
You harden the tip of a stick in the fire until it is your first digging stick.
Keep it
It is not beautiful, but it is yours, and you use it every day.
Show it to the grown-ups
The grown-ups laugh fondly and show you a better way.
Make a better one
The second is much better, the third better still.
Your first fishhook
For days you grind a pearl shell with stone until you have your first little curved hook.
Go fish the reef at once
Your first fish is tiny, but the whole house shares it.
Give it to your grandmother
She hangs it on a cord around her neck and wears it until she dies.
Make many more
Your hands begin to know each kind of shell.
The bone awl
You rub a deer’s leg bone on sandstone to a point, and use it to pierce hide for the first time.
Help your mother sew
That winter your sibling’s coat is warmer, because of the holes you made.
Carve a pattern on the handle
The zigzag on the bone is the first pattern you ever invented.
The first time with the herd alone
For the first time, the grown-ups send you alone to take the herd up to the hill pastures, half a day from the village.
Sleep out on the hill with the herd
That night a wolf takes one. You cry, but no one blames you.
You count the herd every dawn. All there. You come home a different person.
Bring them home before dark
The animals do not graze their fill, but every one is safe.
Goods from far away
A stranger carries in glossy black obsidian from a volcano dozens of days’ walk away.
People from the north bring pale green jade earrings to trade.
People from the southern mountains bring blue-green stone beads to trade.
People from the coast bring up shells no one here has ever seen.
Obsidian from the volcanoes of Cappadocia in Anatolia travelled over 800 km to the Levant; archaeologists trace its source from the stone’s chemistry.
Jade earrings of the Xinglongwa culture in northeast China, about 8,000 years old, are among the oldest jade objects.
Trade food or animals for it
The piece has everyone in the village wanting to visit your house.
Ask the way to where it came from
The stranger draws the route in the dirt. You memorise every line.
Not interested
You look at it a moment, then go back to work.
The last harvest
Your back aches too much to bend for the harvest now, yet this season you still want to go to the fields.
Go out with the grandchildren
You cut only a few handfuls, but the grandchildren hear a story with every one.
Sort the seed grain at home
You pick the best seed for next year, as your mother once did.

You build your family a new house with your own hands

In early farming villages some tasks began to have people who mainly did them, such as potting, knapping or herding, but most people still did many things. Full-time crafts like those of city artisans came later, when surplus food could feed people who did not produce it.
What will you learn
Several adults think you are old enough to learn a real trade, and each wants you as their helper.
You go on helping everyone as before.
Seeds that do not fall
At harvest you notice some plants whose ears do not shatter like the rest: the seeds stay on until you cut them.

Wild wheat and barley drop their seed when ripe. Mutant plants whose ears stay intact were more often carried home and sown again, without anyone meaning to; it took thousands of years for whole fields to be like this.
Save seed from those plants to sow next year
Selected seed that does not shatter
In the years that follow, your plots yield more than anyone’s.
Mix it in with the rest as usual
Your fields stay as they were.
The summer pastures
This summer the grass round the village dries early. The mountain pastures are still green, but it means days of walking and a month sleeping in the open.
Moving herds to high pastures with the seasons is still done in the Zagros and Anatolia today; archaeologists use isotopes in animal teeth to learn when it began.
Take the herd up
The herd comes down fat, with several newborns.
Feed them stored straw
The herd thins but stays safe.
The kiln
Half the pots crack in the fire, shards everywhere.
Mixing sand, straw or crushed shell into the clay keeps pots from cracking in the heat; archaeologists use these tempers to tell potting traditions apart.
Try mixing sand and straw into the clay
In the next firing barely a pot cracks.
They still crack, but you learn that clay differs from place to place.
Dig clay from another riverbank
The new clay is stickier, and stays on your hands for days.
Fire only on still days
You make fewer pots, but fewer break.
The mountain of black stone
You hear the sharpest glossy black stone comes from a volcano far to the north. No one in the village has ever been there.
Obsidian from central Anatolian volcanoes turns up as far as the Levant and the Zagros; this exchange network is older than farming.
Make the journey
You fall on the way and spend months healing in a strangers’ village.
Reached the obsidian source
You come home with a bag of black stone and stories no one has heard.
Wait to trade with travellers
You get little stone, but you are safe.
A house on the old house
A family asks you to build them a new house right on top of their ancestors’ old one, with the dead still buried beneath the floor.
At Çatalhöyük houses were rebuilt in the same spot layer upon layer, some for centuries, until the village became a tall mound.
Rebuild exactly to the old plan
Hearth, sleeping platform and wall reliefs sit exactly where they were; the family weeps with joy.
Try a new, larger design
The new house is brighter, and soon every family wants one like it.
The elders are unhappy that you changed the ancestors’ house.
Colour in the cloth
You wonder whether boiling fibre with red roots or ochre would colour the cloth.
Try boiling it with roots
The cloth comes out reddish orange, and everyone wants some.
The colour washes out, but you are not giving up.
Use woven patterns instead of colour
The braided pattern you invent spreads through the village.
A broken leg
A young man falls from a roof; his leg is badly broken. Everyone looks at you.
Many ancient skeletons show broken bones that healed, meaning someone cared for the injured for weeks; archaeologists see this as evidence of compassion.
Pull the bone straight and splint it
He walks again the next season, though with a limp for life.
His leg sets crooked. You never forget his cries that night.
Let his family tend him the old way
He survives but never walks again; his family cares for him into old age.
Your first apprentice
A child follows you every day and asks to be your apprentice.
Take them on and teach everything
Teach some, keep your secrets
People still have to come to you, for there are things only you can do.
a lion

a big crocodile at the water’s edge

a huge cave bear

A hand on the rock
You grind a blood-red stone to powder, mix it with spit in your mouth, and lay your hand flat on the rock.

The red of ancient hand stencils comes from iron oxide, such as hematite in ochre, ground with water and blown from the mouth. The oldest known hand stencil, on Muna island in Indonesia, is at least about 67,800 years old (announced in 2026).
Blow red iron-oxide pigment around your hand
Left a red hand stencil on the rock
When you lift your hand, its shadow glows red on the stone. It will outlast everyone you know.
Use charcoal from the fire instead
Left a black hand stencil on the rock
The black hand is fainter than red, but it is yours.
Dip your hand in pigment and press it on
Pressed a handprint onto the rock
A solid red palm print, every line of your fingers clear.
A small hand beside yours
Your child wants to leave a handprint on the rock, like you.
Many stencilled hands in Ice Age caves are small; some researchers suggest children and women made more cave art than once thought.
Blow red ochre around the child’s hand beside yours
Stencilled your child’s hand beside your own
A small hand and a large one, side by side on the stone. Your child laughs until red pigment smears their face.
Let the child stencil your hand instead
Pigment sprays everywhere and your hand comes out crooked, but you love it most of all.
The vision
After days of fasting and fever you see something clearer than a dream: the ancestors stand by the fire and tell a story no one has ever heard.

Religions with prophets came long after this age; Stone Age spiritual leaders were more likely shamans or ritual leaders. A woman buried at Hilazon Tachtit, Israel, about 12,000 years ago, lay with some 50 tortoise shells; archaeologists suggest she may have been a shaman.
Tell the whole band the vision
Became the band’s ritual leader
Everyone listens in silence until the fire burns low. From that night, at every rite, everyone turns to you.
Keep it to yourself
You tell it to yourself night after night, and never forget it.
Calling the rain
The rain has stayed away so long that everyone comes asking you to lead a rite.
Lead three nights of rain dancing
On the third night thunder rolls in from the west, and the rain truly falls.
No rain comes. Some begin to whisper that your visions are false.
Tell everyone to follow the rain clouds instead of waiting
You read the clouds right. Two days away is a plain the rain has just reached.
The healing rite
A child is gravely ill. The family begs you to perform a healing rite.
Sing all night and brew herbs as well
At dawn the child opens their eyes. Everyone believes your song called the child’s spirit back.
The child does not wake. The family still thanks you for staying all night.
Say honestly that you may not be able to help
The family nods. You sit with them as an ordinary person.
Someone doubts your visions
A man stands in the middle of the rite and says before everyone that your visions are only a hungry person’s dreams.
Tell a new vision before everyone
Your story silences everyone. Even the challenger sits down.
The band stopped believing your visions
People turn away. From that day no one asks you to lead a rite.
Admit you may be wrong
Your humility earns more respect, even if fewer believe the visions.
Drive the challenger out of the band
He leaves with his family. The rest go quiet, but that quiet is not belief.
People come from many bands to listen
Word of your visions has travelled far. People from bands you have never met walk for days to hear you.
Shared stories and rites let large numbers of strangers cooperate; many scholars see this as a root of later religions.
Tell the ancestors’ story with your vision woven in
Became a visionary heeded by many bands
People from many bands carry your story home. Years later you hear it from strangers’ lips.
✦ Declare that the ancestors chose you as their messenger
Hailed as a prophet ✦
That night a shooting star crosses the sky. Everyone there believes it is the sign.
Send them home to tell it themselves
You do not want anyone walking far for you. Stories should belong to everyone.
A funeral
A beloved elder dies on a rainy night. The band must decide how to send them on.
A hunter does not wake after a long sickness. Everyone gathers around the body.
The old woman who taught everyone the plants dies peacefully.
Lost in the storm
The rain is so heavy you cannot see the camp. You have lost the adults, and the thunder shakes the ground.
Shelter under a big rock and wait it out
By morning the rain stops and you follow the smoke home. The adults praise your calm.
Keep walking the way you think is right
You guess right and reach camp before dark.
You walk the wrong way all night. The adults find you at dawn, shivering and soaked.
Keep shouting
Your voice carries far enough for your mother to hear. She hugs you so hard you can barely breathe.
Your first tool
You knap all day until you strike your first flake sharp enough to really cut hide.
You carry it everywhere and sharpen it every evening.
Give it to your mother
She uses it to cut meat that night and tells everyone who made it.
Keep knapping until your fingers bleed
Your hands hurt for days, but the second flake is far sharper than the first.
Your little sibling is sick
Your youngest sibling has burned with fever for two days and will not eat. The adults are all out foraging.
Sit up all night giving sips of water
By morning the fever breaks. Your sibling opens their eyes and smiles at you.
Your sibling grows weaker. The adults come back in time and tell you that you did all you could.
Fetch the leaves the elders use for fever
You pick the right plant. The elder nods and boils it for your sibling.
You picked the wrong one. The elder throws it away and shows you the right leaf.
Red earth in the cliff
You find a seam of deep red earth in a crack in the cliff. It rubs off on your hands like blood.
Carry it back to the band
The adults are thrilled. Ochre like this trades well.
Paint yourselves with your friends
The whole pack of children turns red. The adults laugh until they cry.
Keep the place a secret
You remember the way and come back for a little at a time, to trade one day.
Learning to swim
The older children leap into deep water, shrieking. You stand at the edge.
Jump in after them
You swallow water and an older child hauls you out, but the next day you try again.
You thrash until you float. That evening you swim across the pool for the first time.
Learn in the shallows with an older sibling
Slow but safe. Your sibling holds your chin above the water.
Something comes by
Freeze and do not move a finger
It stares at you for an age, then moves on.
It lunges. You come away hurt, but the adults drive it off in time.
Run to the adults as fast as you can
You run faster than ever in your life and get there first.
It chases a few steps. You fall and get hurt, but it stops when the adults shout.
Shout and throw stones
It flinches and backs away. The other children look at you differently now.
It gets angry and charges. You are badly hurt.
Strangers in the night
In the dead of night, people from another band burst in to take food and hides. Everyone wakes shouting.
Evidence of violence between groups is real in the Stone Age, such as the Jebel Sahaba cemetery in Sudan, about 13,000 years old.
Hide the little ones in the bushes
You hold the little ones quiet until the noise fades. No one in the bushes is hurt.
Run to wake the adults sleeping farther off
You are knocked down on the way, but the adults wake in time and drive them off.
The adults wake in time. The raiders flee with only a little food.
The great wind
A wind that will not stop. The hides covering the shelter begin to fly.
Help the adults hold the hides down
You cling to the hide until your arms shake. The shelter holds.
Chase the things that blow away
You chase far enough to bring back a big hide.
Things fly too far to follow, but you learn which way this season’s wind blows.
The burning sun
For weeks the sun blazes. The water hole near camp is down to mud.
Follow an elder to dig for water in a dry stream
The elder digs into the sand at the stream’s bend and water slowly seeps up. You will remember this all your life.
Lie in the rock’s shade all day
You watch the shadow creep and learn when the heat will ease.
The tall clouds
An elder points to the tall clouds that build every afternoon and asks what you think they are saying.
Study the shapes carefully
You start to guess when rain will come. The adults begin to ask you.
Say it looks like a bird and run off to play
The elder laughs. That afternoon the rain catches you out on the plain.
The first snow
This morning everything is white. The year’s first snow fell all night.
Help pile snow into a windbreak
The shelter is much warmer. The adults say you are useful this year.
Follow the animal tracks in the snow
Snow tells everything. You lead the adults to a string of hares.
Lightning
Lightning strikes a big tree near camp. Flames rise in the rain.
Help the adults carry embers back
A hot coal burns your hand, but the band’s new fire roars from the embers you carried.
You carry a burning branch home with great care. Everyone calls it your fire.
Run to the water
From the water’s edge you watch the tree burn until the rain puts it out.
The sun is swallowed
At midday the sky slowly darkens. The sun becomes a glowing ring. The birds fall silent.
A total solar eclipse passes over the same spot only once every few hundred years on average. Many people see one once in a lifetime, or never.
Hide your face against your mother
When you look up the light is back. Your mother is still holding you tight.
Watch the elders sing the light back
The elders sing without stopping, and the light truly returns. You will tell this story until you are old.
Remembering the way
The adults are lost in the fog, arguing over the way. You remember passing a fallen tree.
Speak up
You lead everyone home. From then on the adults listen to you more.
Stay quiet; you are only a child
By the time they find the way it is dark. You wish you had spoken.
A lullaby
A baby in the band cries all night and nobody can settle it.
Sing the song your mother sang to you
The baby quiets and sleeps. Several adults sit listening until the song ends.
Make up a new song
Your song is so catchy the other children sing it for years.
A bone toy
With a stone chip you carve a bird bone into a little whistle.
Give it to a younger child
The whistle shrills through camp all season. Nobody complains once.
Trade it to an adult
An adult gives you a shell bead for it.
A snake in the leaves
Your sibling reaches for fruit in a pile of leaves. You see something move beneath.
Yank your sibling back
A venomous snake slides out where the hand just was. The adults talk about it all night.
Shout a warning
Your sibling jumps back in time and the snake slides away.
The reef at low tide
The tide is so low the reef shows. You hunt for shellfish with the other children.
Go all the way to the reef’s edge
You step on a sea urchin. Your foot swells for days.
At the edge are big shellfish no one has taken, and you bring home a beautiful shell.
Stay near shore with the others
The basket is full before the tide turns, and everyone comes back together.
Your first mammoth
For the first time you see a mammoth up close. It is bigger than the whole shelter.
Watch until it walks out of sight
You remember everything: its breath, its smell, its hair blowing in the wind.
Run to tell the hunters
The hunters ruffle your hair and take you to see its tracks the next day.
Walking alone
The adults send you alone on a three-day walk to carry news to kin in another band.
Take the shortcut over the hills
You are lost two days in the hills and arrive late and thinner.
You arrive early. Your kin over there never forget you.
Follow the path everyone uses
On the way you meet someone from another band and talk the whole way.
The dance by the fire
Many bands gather in the season of plenty. Tonight everyone dances around a great fire.
Seasonal gatherings of many bands are a time to trade, find partners and hold ceremonies, found in many hunter-gatherer societies.
Dance till dawn
Someone dances beside you all night. You still remember that smile.
Sit and talk with strangers
You make a friend from a band that lives far away.
A teacher from another band
A craftsperson from another band sees your work and offers to teach you if you live with them for a season.
Go for a season
You come home with techniques no one in your band has seen.
Stay with your own band
You thank them and keep learning from your own elders.
The fire comes
A wildfire reaches camp faster than anyone expected. A child is still in a shelter.
Run in and bring the child out
You get the child out, but your leg is badly burned. Everyone calls you brave.
Saved a child from a wildfire
You carry the child out just before the shelter burns. The mother weeps and holds you.
Shout for the adults
The adults arrive in time and get the child out.
A trading trip
The adults will walk for days to trade with a distant band, and they invite you along.
You see places you have never seen and come back with something rare.
Stay and help at home
There is more work at home than you thought, but everyone knows they can count on you.
The names of the stars
On a clear night an elder points to the stars one by one and tells who each one is.
Ask where the stars come from
The elder tells stories deep into the night. You remember every word.
Learn which stars rise in which season
From then on you know when the herds will move just from the sky.
Stampede
Something spooks the herd, and it thunders straight toward you.
Dive behind a boulder
Dust everywhere. The herd pours past you like a river.
Spear one that falls in the crush
You take a whole animal without a hunt. Everyone eats well for days.
You are trampled and crack a rib.
Defending the camp
A group arrives with spears, demanding a share of your band’s water.
Stand at the front with the adults
A short clash. You are wounded, but they withdraw.
Seeing your band will not back down, they turn away.
Take the children and elders to safety
Everyone you lead away is safe. The adults talk until the water is shared.
Coming of age
It is time to pass your coming-of-age rite before everyone.
Paint your body and fast three days in the wild
You return thinner but standing tall. The adults greet you as an equal.
Sing a song you made, before everyone
The whole band joins the last verse. Your song now belongs to everyone.
The fruit no one eats
There is a purple fruit no one in the band dares eat. You badly want to know what it tastes like.
Take a tiny bite
It is sweet and harmless. The band has one more food from then on.
You vomit all night, but now everyone knows not to eat it.
Let an animal try it first
You watch birds eat it for days. They are fine.
The runner
Urgent news must reach the next band before dusk. Everyone looks at you.
Run at once
You run all afternoon and arrive before sunset. Your news lets them escape a flood in time.
Run together with a friend
You take turns leading, arrive together and laugh until you get your breath back.
Fever in the band
One by one the band falls sick with the same fever, until fewer than half are well.
Move the sick to another shelter and nurse them
You nurse them all back, then fall sick yourself.
The sick recover one by one. You never fall ill.
Take your family to camp apart for a while
Your family stays safe, but some in the band do not forget where you were when they were sick.
Brew herbs for everyone
Your herbs really help. The fever falls faster than anyone expected.
You do not know enough plants yet, but your care comforts everyone.
The hungry year
Food is so short the children have started crying at night.
Ask your friends in other bands for help
You have no friends in other bands to ask. You promise yourself it will not happen again.
Give your share to the children first
You grow thin enough to count your ribs, but every child in the band gets through the season.
Hunt farther than ever before
Three days out is a herd no one hunts. You come home with meat.
You come back empty-handed and barely able to walk.
Stone from far away
Word comes that dozens of days’ walk away, a band has the finest stone for blades.
Obsidian and fine stone travelled hundreds of kilometres from their sources, by journeys and by trade passed hand to hand.
Make the journey yourself
You fall badly ill on the way and must turn back.
Travelled far to trade for fine stone
You come home with the sharpest stone the band has ever seen, and a new friend.
Send goods with a friend from another band
Months later the fine stone reaches you, passed through many hands.
You have neither the goods nor a friend to send them with.
Two families quarrel
Two families fight over sharing meat until one threatens to leave the band.
Step in to mediate
You let both sides talk themselves out, then eat together. No one leaves that night.
Both sides turn their anger on you. One family leaves to start its own band.
Side with your own family
Your family is pleased, but the other side will remember for a long time.
Let time sort it out
The anger fades by itself after several seasons.
The water rises fast
It has rained upstream for days. The river rises so fast you can see it every time you look.
Carry the food uphill first
All the food is saved, but several shelters wash away.
Get the elders and children uphill first
Everyone is safe. The stored food floats away, but no one says a word against you.
A stranger asks to join
A man walks in alone. He says his band has scattered.
Welcome him in
He brings a strange fever. You are sick a long time, but he truly becomes one of you.
He knows plants and routes none of you know, and he teaches all of it.
Feed him and send him on
He thanks you and disappears into the grassland at dawn.
A child follows you everywhere, wanting to learn what you do well.
Teach everything you know
Took a first apprentice
Years later the child is better than you. It makes you prouder than your own skill ever did.
Send them off to play
The child walks off quietly and never asks again.
The fight over water
The drought brings another band to your water hole. Both sides hold spears.
Negotiate to share the water
The bands agree to use the water on alternate days. By the end of the drought you have a friend among them.
The talks fail. There is a short clash before they withdraw.
They fight back. You are badly wounded.
They back off to find other water.
Give up the water hole and move on
Your band walks farther, but nobody gets hurt.
Storm in the night
A great storm comes in the night. A tree crashes beside the shelter and the roof begins to leak.
Hold up the shelter poles all night
Your arms give out by dawn, but the shelter never falls on anyone.
Lead everyone to shelter under the cliff
Under the cliff it is dry and safe. Everyone listens to the storm until morning.
Reading the sky
Everyone is ready for a long hunt, but you notice the clouds and wind are strange today.
Tell everyone to wait
That afternoon a great storm sweeps the plain they were heading for. No one hunts without asking you again.
The storm catches everyone in the open. They come home soaked and shivering.
A masterpiece
You spend a whole season making the finest thing of your life.
Keep it for your descendants
Made a masterpiece
It is handed down in the family for generations.
Trade it to a distant band
Your name travels farther than you ever will.
The song everyone sings
At a great gathering, someone asks you to sing before many bands.
Sing the ancestors’ old song
People from other bands sing along, because the song is older than any band.
Sing a new song of your own
Years later you hear strangers singing your song.
Who will carry it on
You know your time is short. Everything you know must pass to someone.
The quickest grandchild
Passed knowledge to a grandchild
The grandchild learns so fast it astonishes you.
The orphan nobody teaches
Taught an orphan no one else would
No one had ever given that child time before. They will never forget you.
To see where you were born
Every night you dream of the place you were born, though it is very far away.
Make the journey back
Walked back to see your birthplace
Everything has changed except the sound of the wind in the same old tree.
Tell the grandchildren about it instead
The grandchildren listen until they fall asleep. One day they might see it themselves.
How the world began
The children ask how the world began. Everyone waits for you.
Tell it as the ancestors told it
Every word is as you heard it as a child. The story passes through you to another generation.
Add your own journeys to it
In the next generation’s telling, there will be someone very like you.
Falling behind
Your knees ache so much you cannot keep up when the band moves camp.
Let the young help you along
The young take turns helping you the whole way, without a word of complaint.
Everyone helps, but you feel like a burden.
Stay to watch the old camp and follow later
You follow slowly over several days, but you get there in the end.
Naming a grandchild
Your first grandchild is born, and the family asks you to choose the name.
Name the child after an ancestor
An old name lives again.
Name the child for something that happened that day
Everyone laughs at the name, but no one forgets the day the child was born.
One last hunt
The young are setting out to hunt. You feel you want to go, just once more.
You are not fast anymore, but you know which way the animal will turn before anyone.
You fall on the plain and the young carry you home.
Stay and wait for their stories
That night they all compete to tell you the story.
Fog so thick you cannot see your own hand. The band waits for it to lift before setting out.
A rainbow arcs over the valley after rain. The children run to catch it.
Thunder all night. The elders say it is the ancestors talking.
Heat enough to crack stone. The band hides under the trees all afternoon.
Hail rattles on the shelter. The children gather it to suck on.
Green light ripples across the night sky. No one dares to sleep.
The northern lights are seen at high latitudes near the poles.
Hundreds of shooting stars streak across the sky in one night.
A whirlwind spins a tall spiral of dust across the plain.
The smell of earth after the first rain fills the land. Everyone comes out to stand in it.
Frost whitens every blade of grass at dawn.
Sea mist rolls in at dawn. The waves are loud, but you cannot see the sea.
The full moon is bright enough to travel by night.
Red dust blows in from the desert for a week. The sky turns orange.
The river freezes hard enough to walk on. The band crosses to hunt the far bank.
Antelope pass in the distance, raising dust all afternoon.

About 5,000 years ago Uruk may have been the largest city in the world, with perhaps 40,000–80,000 people. The earliest inscribed tablets come from the Eanna temple of the goddess Inanna. Legend says the city’s wall, some 9 km long, was built by Gilgamesh.

At Ur in the 1920s the archaeologist Leonard Woolley excavated the Royal Cemetery, about 4,600 years old, including the tomb of Queen Puabi. The city’s great ziggurat was built by King Ur-Nammu around 2100 BCE.
Lagash and neighbouring Umma fought over the border fields for generations; the Stele of the Vultures records a Lagash victory. Many stone statues of its ruler Gudea were found here.

Nippur was the religious heart of Sumer, home of the god Enlil, but never a political capital. Huge numbers of school tablets were found here; much of the Sumerian literature we know comes from Nippur.
The Sumerian King List says that after the great flood, kingship first came down from heaven at Kish. The same list names Kubaba, a woman tavern keeper who became king of Kish.

At Sippar lived the naditu women of the god Shamash. They did not marry and lived in a cloister of the temple, yet they bought land, lent silver and made contracts in their own names; thousands of tablets record their business.
Babylon rose under Hammurabi (about 1792–1750 BCE) and was greatest under Nebuchadnezzar II (604–562 BCE), who built the Ishtar Gate.

Mesopotamian society was layered. Hammurabi’s laws distinguish free citizens, commoners and slaves, and the same offence carried different penalties. Many people worked for a temple or palace in return for rations. Some slaves were war captives; others fell into slavery through debt.

Ordinary people were listed in ration lists, contracts and receipts, so we know the names of tens of thousands of Mesopotamians who were not kings.

Hammurabi’s law 117 says that a person sold or bound into service for a debt must be freed in the fourth year.
In Mesopotamia a person who could not repay might have to work for the creditor, or sell a child or themselves into debt slavery.

The term is over. You go home a free person again.
Freed from debt bondage
The ruler Uru-inimgina proclaims debts forgiven, and forbids the powerful to seize the donkeys, houses and fish of the poor.

The reform texts of Uru-inimgina of Lagash, about 2350 BCE, use the word amargi, literally “return to the mother”, for releasing people from debt. It is often called the oldest written word for “freedom”.
Word comes that a man named Sargon of Akkad is taking the Sumerian cities one by one and tearing down their walls.
Sargon of Akkad (about 2334–2279 BCE) united Mesopotamia into the first empire we know of. Akkadian began to replace Sumerian in government.
For years in a row the northern rains fail, the rivers fall, and herders from the mountains raid the plains for food.

About 4,200 years ago much of the world turned severely dry. Many scholars link it to the fall of the Akkadian Empire and the arrival of the Gutians from the Zagros, though how much it caused is debated.
The whole city lays millions of bricks into a stepped mountain for the moon god. King Ur-Nammu comes to watch.
The Great Ziggurat of Ur was built about 2100 BCE, a core of mud brick faced with baked brick set in bitumen. Its restored base still stands in Iraq today.
An army from Elam breaks into the city. The temples burn; people are killed and carried off; the king is led away a captive.
Ur was sacked by the Elamites about 2004 BCE. The poem known as the Lament for Ur mourns bodies lying in the city gates. Fires that burned cities sometimes baked clay tablets hard and preserved them.
An official reads King Hammurabi’s laws aloud in the market. Each begins: “If a man…”
Hammurabi’s code, about 1754 BCE, has some 282 laws carved on a black stone stele over two metres tall, now in the Louvre. Older law collections exist too, such as Ur-Nammu’s, about 2100 BCE.
A Hittite army from far away storms Babylon, loots the temples and carries off the statue of Marduk.
About 1595 BCE the Hittite king Mursili I sacked Babylon, ending Hammurabi’s dynasty.
Captives from Judah are settled by the canals outside the city. In the evenings you hear them singing sad songs about home.
Nebuchadnezzar II took Jerusalem in 597 and 586 BCE and deported many Judeans to Babylonia. Psalm 137 begins “By the rivers of Babylon”.
The Persian army of King Cyrus enters Babylon almost without a fight, and the priests of Marduk welcome the new king.
In 539 BCE Cyrus the Great took Babylon; the Cyrus Cylinder claims Marduk chose him. Babylon never again ruled an empire of its own, but people went on writing cuneiform there for centuries.

Mesopotamians measured value in silver, by weight. A shekel weighed about 8 grams; in the Old Babylonian period a month’s hired labour cost about one shekel. In daily life people often paid in barley.

Mesopotamian letters were written on palm-sized clay tablets, then wrapped in a clay envelope bearing the addressee’s name and a seal. People who could not read hired a scribe to write and read for them. Papyrus was Egypt’s writing material and was rarely used in Mesopotamia.

The scribal school was the edubba, “tablet house”. Pupils began with wedges, then copied sign lists, word lists, proverbs and finally literature. Most were sons of well-off families, but there were women scribes too.

Literacy in Mesopotamia was very rare, perhaps fewer than one person in a hundred. Learning took years because hundreds of signs had to be memorised; most people hired a scribe when something had to be written.

Mesopotamians drank beer every day; children drank weak beer, and workers received beer as part of their wages. Some of the oldest chemical traces of barley beer come from Godin Tepe in Iran, about 5,000 years old.

Your grandfather gives you a small stone cylinder seal. Rolled across clay, it leaves a long row of people, animals and gods.
Cylinder seals were used from about 3500 BCE. They worked like signatures, sealing contracts, jar stoppers and storeroom doors. Many people wore theirs on a cord around the neck.

Snow melts in the northern mountains, and the river rises just at harvest time. Every adult runs to raise the levees.

Unlike the Nile’s regular flood, the Tigris and Euphrates rose in April and May, just as the grain ripened, and unpredictably. Mesopotamians had to dig canals and levees endlessly, and told many stories of a great flood.

In the morning the levee holds; your family’s barley is saved.

The shepherd counts sheep with little clay tokens, one token for each sheep, and seals them all inside a clay ball so they can be checked when the flock comes back.

The archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat proposed that cuneiform grew out of counting tokens like these, once people began pressing the tokens’ shapes onto the outside of the clay balls instead of breaking them open. The idea is widely cited but still debated.

You count every one right, and the shepherd gives you a sheep-shaped token to keep.

The adults look at the marks and say: this way no one has to break the ball at all.

Lions once lived in Mesopotamia; Assyrian and Babylonian kings boasted of lion hunts in inscriptions and reliefs. The last Asiatic lions in Iraq vanished in the 20th century.

“Friendship lasts a day; kinship lasts forever.”
The teacher says this one is a favourite, and asks whether you agree.
“A scribe whose hand keeps up with the mouth: now that is a scribe!”

Babylonians counted in base sixty, which is why we still have 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle. The tablet Plimpton 322, about 1800 BCE, lists numbers matching what was later called the Pythagorean theorem, more than a thousand years before Pythagoras.

Mesopotamian marriages were usually arranged by families. The groom’s side paid a bride-price and the bride brought a dowry that remained hers. Many couples had written contracts, some even setting the penalty for divorce.

The king calls up young men from every house. Each gets a spear, a wooden shield and three loaves of bread.

The Stele of the Vultures, about 2450 BCE, shows Lagash soldiers marching in a tight block behind their shields with spears thrust forward, one of the oldest images of an organised army. The Lagash–Umma border war dragged on for about a century.

Mesopotamian beer had husks floating in it, so people drank through long straws. Queen Puabi’s tomb at Ur held a drinking straw of gold and lapis lazuli, and many seals show people drinking from a shared jar.

Old Babylonian law capped interest at about 33 per cent a year on barley and 20 per cent on silver. Debt was very common, and some kings proclaimed a misharum, cancelling debts across the land so that too many people did not fall into debt slavery.

You write: “Who do you take me for, to treat me like this?” Ea-nasir never answers. Your letter likely joins the pile in his house.

Hammurabi’s law 53 says that if a man neglects his dike and it floods others’ fields, he must replace the grain he destroyed; if he cannot, he and his goods are sold to pay for it.

Next year your neighbour ploughs your field, and mends his own dike too.

Tales of Gilgamesh
In the tavern an old man tells of Gilgamesh, the king of Uruk who built its walls, and Enkidu, the friend the gods made from clay in the wild.
Gilgamesh may have been a real king of Uruk around 2700 BCE. Sumerian poems about him were written down around 2100 BCE; the full Akkadian epic came centuries later.

You tell the children about Enkidu until they fall asleep.

The old man points to the city wall. “Well, who else built that?”
Siduri’s advice

You read the part where Gilgamesh searches for eternal life. A tavern keeper named Siduri tells him the gods kept life without death for themselves; a person should eat well, dance, bathe, wear clean clothes, cherish the child holding their hand, and let their beloved delight in their embrace.
Siduri’s speech survives on an Old Babylonian tablet from Sippar, about 1800 BCE; it was dropped from the later standard version. The game retells it in new words.
Live as Siduri says
You stop work an hour earlier each day to sit with the children by the canal.
Make something that will outlast you, like the walls of Uruk
You decide your name will live in your work.
