You begin asking questions that make the priests uneasy.
Gardens on the terraces
Word in the palace is that the king will raise a garden on high terraces, planting mountain trees for a queen homesick for her hills. The problem is how to lift the water to the top.

The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, yet no Babylonian tablet mentions them. The story, including the homesick queen, comes from Greek and Roman writers centuries later. The scholar Stephanie Dalley argued the gardens were at Nineveh, built by King Sennacherib. Whether they existed is still debated.
A loop of buckets on a chain, turned by men
Helped build the terrace gardens
It takes men turning the wheel day and night, but the next year the trees on top break into leaf.
Try a giant spiral of copper that turns and draws water up
Devised a water-lifter for the royal garden
The casters say it cannot be done, until water spills out at the top for the first time.
The first spiral cracks in casting, and talents of copper are wasted.
Say such a garden is not worth the labour
No one listens; the building starts without you.
Blue glazed bricks
The royal craftsmen need help firing deep blue glazed bricks moulded with lions, wild bulls and mushhushshu dragons, for the new gate of the goddess Ishtar.
The Ishtar Gate was built about 575 BCE under Nebuchadnezzar II. Excavated pieces were rebuilt in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin.
Work at the kilns
Fired bricks for the Ishtar Gate
Every time you pass the gate, you look for the lion you helped fire.
Watch the New Year procession
The statue of Marduk is carried through the blue gate; the crowd falls silent.
The Akitu festival
At the New Year festival you see the high priest strip the king of his regalia and strike his face before Marduk. Everyone watches to see whether the king’s tears will flow.
In Babylon’s Akitu rite the high priest struck the king; if tears came, Marduk was pleased and the year would be good. Each year the king had to accept that his power came from the god.
Pray for the tears to come
The tears come, and the crowd roars with joy.
No tears. People go home uneasy.
Neighbours from far away
A family of Judean captives settles near your house. They speak another tongue, worship one god, and will not eat certain foods.
Many Judeans were deported to Babylonia after 597 and 586 BCE. Some worked, traded and settled for generations; tablets from a town called “Judah-town” record their daily lives.
Help them find work
Listen to their songs
One song tells of hanging harps on the willows by the river. You remember the tune all your life.
Keep your distance
You never really know them.
Reading the liver
Before the king marches, the priests slaughter a sheep and call you to help read the shape of its liver for the gods’ answer.
Reading sheep’s livers was a central skill of Babylonian priests. Clay models of livers inscribed with omens have been found, and thousands of omen tablets were copied for centuries.
Read it as favourable
The army wins, and everyone says the liver never lies.
The army is beaten, and some begin to look at you with doubt.
Read it as ill: wait
The king waits a month, then orders a new reading.
This month’s ration
The official measures out half as much barley for the women as for the men, though you weave all day just as they work.
The official measures your barley several cups short, saying the temple is short this year too.
Ration lists of the Third Dynasty of Ur give male workers about 60 sila of barley a month, women about 30, and children less. Temples and palaces employed thousands of women weavers.
Go with the others to complain to the overseer
The overseer adds a cup each. Not much, but a victory.
The loudest of you is beaten, and you get nothing more.
Accept it in silence
As every month, you feed the children before yourself.
Buying freedom
For years you have saved silver from extra work, until you have enough to redeem yourself. Your master hesitates a long time.
Some Mesopotamian slaves held property, did business and could buy their freedom; others were freed by adoption. Some release contracts say “his forehead is cleared”.
Offer all of it
Bought your own freedom
The scribe writes the contract: “his forehead is cleared.” You walk out a free person.
Your master keeps part of the silver and says it is not yet enough.
An adopted child
You have no child to care for you in old age. A poor neighbour has seven children and is willing to let you adopt one.
Adoption was common in Mesopotamia and recorded in written contracts: the child had to support the parents in old age and perform their rites after death, and the parents had to leave an inheritance.
Adopt, with a contract
Adopted a child
The child calls you mother or father from the first night.
Decline
Your house stays as quiet as before.
The diary of the sky
Tonight Jupiter draws close to the moon. Your master tells you to record everything you see: the stars, the price of barley and the river’s level.

Babylonian astronomers kept “astronomical diaries” from about 652 BCE into the first century BCE, the longest continuous scientific record of the ancient world. From the cycles they recorded, they could predict eclipses.
Record every night without fail
Kept the diary of the sky for Babylon’s astronomers
Two years later you predict a lunar eclipse correctly for the first time.
Care more for the omens than the numbers
You read omens to the palace, which likes them better than numbers.
The hymns of Enheduanna
You are given a hymn to Inanna to copy. Its author is Enheduanna, daughter of King Sargon and high priestess of the moon god at Ur.
Enheduanna (about 2285–2250 BCE) is often called the first author known by name. Her hymns were copied in scribal schools for centuries, though some scholars doubt she wrote all of them.
Learn it by heart
That night you recite the hymn in the dark, your voice shaking.
Write a hymn of your own
Wrote a hymn of your own
You hide the tablet under your bed and dare not show anyone.
A ship to Dilmun
A ship loaded with wool and oil is about to sail down the Gulf to Dilmun, and on to Magan, to trade for copper. The merchants invite you to invest.

Dilmun (today’s Bahrain) was a key trading port. Copper came from Magan (today’s Oman), and some goods came from Meluhha, the Indus Valley; Indus-style seals found at Ur show the two civilisations were linked by sea.
Invest
The ship returns full of copper, and your silver nearly triples.
The ship never returns, and no one learns why.
Sail with it yourself
Sailed to Dilmun to trade
You see the open sea for the first time, and people from Meluhha speaking a language no one understands.
A storm in the Gulf nearly sinks the ship. You come home feverish and empty-handed.
Do not risk it
You stay home, and so does your silver.
Fields turning white
White patches crust your field, and the wheat comes up thinner every year. The elders say the soil is turning salty.

Centuries of irrigation built up salt in the soils of southern Mesopotamia. Some scholars argue farmers shifted from wheat to the more salt-tolerant barley, but how much salt caused the decline of the southern cities is debated.
Give up wheat for barley
The barley does better, though it fetches less.
Let the field lie fallow a year
The next year the soil is a little better.
From the tavern to the throne
Kish has no king. People who have drunk in your tavern for decades crowd the door and call on you to rule the city.

The Sumerian King List says Kubaba, “the woman tavern keeper”, became king of Kish and reigned 100 years. She is the only woman in the list to rule in her own right, but the list mixes legend and history, so no one knows if she was real.
Take the throne ✦
ruler of Kish, once a tavern keeper ✦
Became ruler of Kish ✦
You rule Kish with the one thing you know: everyone must eat and drink fairly.
Refuse, and go back to brewing
Everyone is disappointed, but your beer is still the best in Kish.
The cupbearer’s dream
You have become the king of Kish’s cupbearer. One night you dream that Inanna drowns the king in a river of blood. Afraid, the king sends you to another city with a sealed tablet.

Legend says Sargon was born to a priestess and set adrift in a reed basket, raised by a water-drawer named Aqqi as a gardener, and became cupbearer to King Ur-Zababa of Kish before seizing power. The game adapts these tales, which were written centuries after Sargon.
Break the tablet to see what it says ✦
founder of a new dynasty ✦
Seized power and founded a dynasty ✦
The tablet orders the bearer’s death. You turn back, gather gardeners and soldiers, and march into Kish as its new king.
Deliver it as ordered
You escape with your life, barely, and never return to Kish.
Physician or exorcist
You have been ill for days. The family argues whether to call an asu, who heals with herbs and bandages, or an ashipu, who drives out the demons believed to cause disease.

Mesopotamians had two kinds of healer: the asu used medicines from plants and minerals and bandages; the ashipu used incantations and rites. Often they worked together. Medical tablets describe symptoms in detail.
Call the asu
The poultice stings bitterly, but the sore begins to heal.
Call the ashipu
The ashipu chants all night, and the family feels much better.
Call both
They work side by side without looking at each other.
Calling the ancestors’ names
Each month the family pours water down a clay pipe set into the floor and calls the ancestors by name, one by one. This year you are the one who calls.
In the Mesopotamian kispum rite the living gave food and water to the dead and called their names. A spirit no one named or fed was believed to wander hungry, so names mattered greatly.
Teach the grandchildren every name
The youngest grandchild recites seven generations of names, including yours.
Add the names of those no one calls
You call the names of old friends who left no children. The family does not understand, but follows you.
Your tablets

Unbaked clay dissolves when wet, but tablets that were fired, on purpose or when a city burned, last for thousands of years. Ashurbanipal’s library at Nineveh survived because the city was burned in 612 BCE. Archaeologists also find private letters kept in jars beneath house floors.
Bake them hard and store them in a jar under the floor
You lay the tablets in the jar one by one, as if burying memories.
Give them to the temple’s tablet room
The priests accept them, and have a young scribe copy some.
Knead them back into clay for the grandchildren to write on
Your grandchild writes a first sign on clay that was once your work.
Dividing the estate
Your children have begun asking who will get the house, the fields and the flock. The eldest says custom gives him more.

In the Old Babylonian period sons shared the estate, with the eldest often taking an extra share; daughters received dowries when they married. Thousands of inheritance tablets survive, and some families quarrelled across generations.
Write a clear will, sharing equally
The eldest is unhappy, but no one goes to court.
Give the eldest more, by custom
Your youngest is silent for days.
Let them settle it among themselves
After you are gone, they hire a scribe to divide the estate three times over.
The wall of Uruk

At the end of the epic, Gilgamesh comes home without eternal life. He invites the boatman to walk the wall of Uruk and look at its fired bricks, its gardens and its clay pits. You read the passage many times.
The epic ends with the same image it began with, the walls of Uruk. Many readers take it to mean that people do not live forever, but what they build and the stories told about them last longer.
Walk the wall of your own city
From the wall you see the roofs, the canals and the fields your generation made.
Write the story of your own life in clay
You manage only three tablets, but every name you loved is in them.
The brewery’s barley account
The head of the temple brewery has you record the barley received over 37 months. You press the numbers into clay and add the responsible official’s name at the bottom.

A Uruk-period tablet of about 3100 BCE records some 29,086 measures of barley over 37 months and ends with the word “Kushim”. Some scholars suggest it may be the oldest written name of a person, though it may be a title instead. Most early writing was accounting, not storytelling.
Record the numbers exactly
The overseer checks it and finds not a single error.
Slip your own name into the corner too
Wrote your own name into a temple account
Your name will stay there longer than you imagine.
A mistake in wet clay
You have written one number wrong in the sheep account, and the clay is still wet.
Scribes could fix wet clay by smoothing it and writing again; once the clay dried or was fired, nothing could be changed. That is why important contracts were baked hard.
Smooth it and rewrite
Your thumbprint stays in the corner of the tablet.
Leave it; no one will notice
The auditor notices and summons you.
No one notices. One sheep vanishes from history.
A two-language word list
No one speaks Sumerian at home any more, but it lives on in temples and literature. Your master has you make a list of Sumerian words beside their Akkadian meanings.

Sumerian stopped being spoken in daily life around 2000–1800 BCE but was used in ritual and learning for nearly two thousand years more, much like Latin in Europe. These bilingual lists later helped modern scholars read Sumerian.
List every word you know
Your list runs to more than seven tablets.
Add the rude words the pupils like to use
Your master laughs until he coughs, then rubs half of them out.
The king’s victory inscription
The king wants an inscription of his latest victory. You know the army took a few small villages, but the king wants it to say five great cities fell.
Mesopotamian royal inscriptions often exaggerate, so historians compare them with accounts, letters and evidence from the other side.
Write what the king wants
The king is pleased. Four thousand years later, historians will doubt your numbers.
Record the truth on a dull account tablet no one reads
The stone boasts; your account tablet records how many sheep were really taken.
The beer turns sour
The heat is fierce, and a whole jar turns sour before it can be sold. Regulars wait at the door.
Mesopotamians made many beers, dark, red and sweet; word lists name more than twenty kinds. Without hops, beer spoiled quickly and had to be drunk within days.
Add dates to sweeten it
Customers say it tastes odd but good; some order it again.
Pour it out and tell them honestly
Your customers trust your tavern more.
Sell it at full price anyway
You make the silver, but the quarter starts talking about your beer.
Short measures
Another tavern keeper shares a trick: pour the beer a little short, and take payment in grain with an oversized measure.
Hammurabi’s law 108 says that if a tavern keeper takes grain by an oversized weight, or gives less beer than the grain’s worth, she shall be thrown into the water.
Your tavern makes less, but you sleep well.
Try it for a month
A customer complains. You are taken to the river and barely survive.
No one finds out, but you flinch whenever someone eyes the measure.
The seeder plough
The plough-team leader has you try a new plough with a funnel that drops seed into the furrow as it goes.
Mesopotamians used seeder ploughs with a funnel from around 2000 BCE or earlier, saving seed. A text called the Farmer’s Instructions describes a year of farm work step by step.
Practise until it is second nature
Your furrows are the straightest in the team, and use half the seed.
Stick to sowing by hand
The leader shakes his head, but your barley still grows.
The temple’s sheep count
The day comes to bring the temple’s flock to the scribes for counting. By contract you owe a set number of lambs and fleeces, but wolves took several this year.

Temple shepherds worked under contracts fixing how many lambs and fleeces they owed, and paid for losses caused by neglect. Hammurabi’s law 266 excused the shepherd if a beast was taken by a lion or died of disease through no fault of his.
Swear before the god it was wild beasts
The scribe records your oath and strikes the shortfall.
Make it up with your own sheep
Your own flock shrinks, but your name in the temple books is clean.
Tin from far away
There is copper enough, but the tin has run out, and the caravan that brings it from mountains far to the east has not come.

Bronze is copper alloyed with about a tenth tin, harder than pure copper. Mesopotamia had neither metal and imported both; tin may have come from as far as Afghanistan or Central Asia. Before tin bronze, smiths used arsenical copper, which poisoned those who smelted it.
Use the old arsenic copper
The furnace fumes leave you coughing all night, but the castings are hard enough.
Wait, and remelt old pieces
You melt broken axes and old pins until you have bronze enough for one job.
Pollinating the palms
An old gardener teaches you to climb the male date palms, cut their flowers and tie them into the female trees.
Mesopotamians pollinated date palms by hand from early times; Assyrian reliefs show it, and several of Hammurabi’s laws concern date orchards, with the gardener taking a share of the harvest.
Climb up yourself
A frond snaps underfoot and you fall, twisting your leg.
That year your palms bear so heavily the branches bow.
Keep track of which trees are done
You tie a coloured thread on each finished tree, and the old gardener nods approval.
The shield wall
The enemy army stands before you. Your captain orders everyone to close up behind their shields and push their spears forward.
Hold the front rank
Your rank does not break, and the enemy falls back.
An enemy spear pierces your shield and cuts your shoulder.
Tend the wounded behind the line
You drag three friends off the field.
You race your friends across the close-packed rooftops while your mother shouts from the courtyard.
You shape a little clay donkey on wheels and drag it all over the courtyard.
Clay toy animals on wheels have been found in many Mesopotamian cities.
Small reed boats bring fish and reeds to the quay in the morning.
At harvest your whole family cuts barley by the canal with clay sickles.
Southern Mesopotamia had almost no stone, so people made sickles of baked clay in great numbers.
A sandstorm blows in from the desert for three days; everyone stays inside with the windows shut.
The whole quarter mends the roofs with reeds and mud before the rains.
A scribe sits at the city gate, writing letters for people who cannot read.
A procession carries the city god’s statue out of the temple while people scatter dates and flour.
A temple ox breaks loose in the market and everyone scrambles onto the roofs.
A donkey caravan laden with tin and cloth comes in through the city gate.
Donkeys were Mesopotamia’s main pack animals; camels came into wide use much later. Donkey caravans traded as far as Anatolia.
Shepherds drive their flocks through the city; the smell of wool fills the street.
You watch a potter spin the wheel fast; a smooth pot rises from the clay in a few breaths.
The potter’s wheel was used in Mesopotamia from about 4500–4000 BCE; wheels for carts came later.
Workers queue for bevelled-rim bowls of barley; identical bowls lie stacked by the thousand.
Bevelled-rim bowls of the Uruk period are found in vast numbers, all made alike; many scholars think they held rations for workers.
At the Eanna temple you see a tall stone vase carved with rows of naked men carrying offerings up to Inanna.
The Warka Vase from Uruk, about 3200–3000 BCE, is one of the oldest narrative carvings. It was stolen from the Iraq Museum in 2003 and later returned.
The queen has died. Dozens of attendants, soldiers and musicians walk down into her tomb with her, and do not come back up.

In the Royal Cemetery of Ur, about 2600–2500 BCE, “death pits” held dozens of attendants around elite burials such as Queen Puabi’s. Studies of some skulls suggest they were killed rather than dying willingly.
A musician plays a lyre with a golden bull’s head at a feast in a great house.
The bull-headed lyres from the Royal Cemetery of Ur, about 2500 BCE, are among the oldest surviving stringed instruments.
A messenger says King Shulgi ran from Nippur to Ur and back in a single day to attend festivals in both cities.
In his own hymns Shulgi claimed to have run some 160 km there and back in one day. He also claimed to have founded scribal schools and to be the finest scribe of all.
A merchant grumbles that he must pay a fine in silver under King Ur-Nammu’s laws for injuring a man.
The Code of Ur-Nammu, about 2100 BCE, is the oldest known law code. It mostly punishes with fines in silver rather than the “eye for an eye” found in some of Hammurabi’s laws.
You hear that by law, if a nobleman blinds another nobleman, his own eye is put out; if he blinds a commoner, he only pays silver.
Hammurabi’s laws 196–199 apply “eye for an eye” only between equals; if the victim was a commoner or a slave, the offender paid silver.
The teacher sets a list of hundreds of names of trees and wooden things, ordered by their first sign.
Word lists like these are among the oldest texts of all, copied almost unchanged for more than two thousand years.
You read how Gilgamesh and Enkidu wrestle until the walls shake, and then become dearest friends.
You read how the two friends travel to the Cedar Forest and kill Humbaba, its guardian.
You read how Enkidu sickens and dies; Gilgamesh will not bury him until a worm falls from his nose, and then begins to fear death.
You read how Utnapishtim tells of the great flood: he built a boat, loaded the animals, and released a dove, a swallow and a raven.

In 1872 the British scholar George Smith read this flood story on a tablet from Nineveh and was overcome with excitement at its likeness to Noah’s ark. Scholars now think the Mesopotamian flood stories are older and influenced the Hebrew account.
You read how Gilgamesh dives for the plant of youth, but while he bathes a snake steals it, sheds its skin and slips away.
In the tavern you hear how Gilgamesh and Enkidu wrestled until the walls shook, and then became dearest friends.
The storyteller tells how the two friends went to the Cedar Forest and killed Humbaba, its guardian.
The whole tavern falls quiet when the storyteller reaches Enkidu’s death, and Gilgamesh’s fear of dying.
An old man tells of the man who survived the great flood in a huge boat and sent out birds to find land.
You hear the hymn to Ninkasi, which tells how to brew beer from baking the bread to filtering it into the jar.
The Hymn to Ninkasi, about 1800 BCE, is both a prayer and something like a brewing recipe. In 1991 a US brewery tried brewing beer by following it.
A naditu buys a field from an indebted farmer and hires him to go on working it.
From the roof you see Marduk’s stepped tower, nearly ninety metres high.
The ziggurat Etemenanki of Babylon, “house of the foundation of heaven and earth”, may have inspired the biblical Tower of Babel. Only traces of its base remain.
The priests announce an eclipse of the moon tonight. The king will stay hidden in the palace while a “substitute king” sits on the throne.

Babylonians and Assyrians believed some eclipses threatened the king, so they enthroned an ordinary man as a temporary “substitute king” to take the evil. Sometimes he was put to death when the rite ended.
Your master hires you out to the temple weavers and keeps your wages.
The feast in the great house has musicians, a storyteller and eighteen dishes.
The tavern argues over who is better, shepherd or farmer, until an old man settles it with an old poem and everyone laughs.
Sumerian literature includes debate poems: shepherd versus farmer, hoe versus plough, bird versus fish, summer versus winter. Scribal pupils copied them.
You help the priests set food and beer before the god’s statue twice a day; in the evening it is shared among the temple household.
Statues in Mesopotamian temples were cared for as if alive, fed, washed and dressed. The offered food was then shared among priests and workers.
You grow onions, cucumbers and beans in the shade under the date palms, where the sun cannot scorch them.
Mesopotamians gardened in layers: tall date palms for shade, fruit trees like pomegranates beneath, and vegetables at the bottom.
You blow through a pipe into the furnace until the copper runs like orange water.
At the quay there is deep blue lapis lazuli from mountains far to the east, and red carnelian from Meluhha.
Mesopotamian lapis lazuli came from Badakhshan in today’s Afghanistan, more than 2,000 km away. Long carnelian beads from the Indus Valley were found in the Royal Cemetery of Ur.
The creditor sends a man to remind you the interest has grown again.
The king proclaims a misharum, cancelling the people’s barley debts across the land. Scribes smash loan tablets in heaps.
Several Babylonian kings proclaimed a misharum (“justice”) on taking the throne or in hard years. A surviving edict of King Ammi-saduqa lists exactly which debts were cancelled.
A great flood breaks the levees and buries fields in mud; the whole city must dig the canals anew.
At Kish and Shuruppak archaeologists found thick flood layers about 2900 BCE. Some link them to the flood stories, but the flood layers in different cities have different dates.
Officials come to collect taxes in barley, wool and days of labour.
You roll your grandfather’s seal across a contract for the first time, signing with a picture.
Your sister’s wedding has date bread, beer and singing all night.
A scribe reads you a letter from a relative in another city. It begins, “May Shamash keep you alive forever.”
Your child comes home from the tablet house complaining the teacher caned them again. You laugh, remembering it happened to you.
Word comes that a neighbouring city has fallen. Refugees pour in with donkeys and children.
Your knees ache so much you sit on a reed mat watching the grandchildren play.
You read an old tablet you wrote as a pupil and laugh at the wobbly hand.
Donkeys bray in the market.
Smoke from the bread ovens rises over the roofs.
A heron stands still in the reed marsh.
The sun bakes the mud-brick walls too hot to touch.
A big sailing boat drifts downriver, loaded with onions and barley.
Children splash in the irrigation canal.
A cool wind comes at night, and everyone sleeps on the roofs.
The date palms hang heavy with golden clusters.
A scribe hurries past with a basket of tablets.
Chanting from the temple carries across the city at dawn.
Mosquitoes swarm after the floodwater recedes.
The temple’s flocks pass through the city gate.
The blue Ishtar Gate gleams in the morning sun.
Hundreds of workers are raising a temple on a high terrace.

Within a few centuries, the marks in clay that began as barley and sheep accounts in your city will become a script for laws, letters and poems. Cuneiform will be used for more than three thousand years, to write more than a dozen languages.

The Sumerian city-states will go on fighting each other for generations, until a man from Akkad named Sargon unites them into the first empire. Your language will slowly vanish from people’s lips, yet live on in schools and temples for two thousand years.

The Akkadian Empire will fall within little more than a century, amid drought and invasion. But the idea of ruling “the four corners of the world” never dies; dozens of later kings will try to repeat it.
The Third Dynasty of Ur was the last age when Sumerian was the language of the state. Tens of thousands of its account tablets survive, some recording the daily rations of ordinary workers.

After Hammurabi, Babylon will be sacked by the Hittites, but his laws will be copied in scribal schools for a thousand years, and the Epic of Gilgamesh will be reworked into the version we read today.

In 539 BCE Persia took Babylon; two centuries later Alexander the Great died here. The city slowly emptied, but Babylonian astronomers went on writing cuneiform until about 75 CE, the last tablet known.
Then no one could read cuneiform for nearly two thousand years, until scholars deciphered it in the 1850s. Hundreds of thousands of tablets have been excavated, and many have never been read.
✦ Legend: the King List records that a woman tavern keeper ruled Kish. No one knows if it was you, or who she was.
✦ Legend: centuries later, people tell of a gardener who became a king.
The terrace garden you helped build will be told of by Greek writers as one of the Seven Wonders of the World, though no one has ever proved where it stood.
If your complaint survived, it may have been dug up in the same pile as Nanni’s letter.
Your dull account tablet tells the truth the king’s inscription hid.
You never wrote, but your name is on someone else’s tablet. If it survived, someone may read your name aloud today.
Your descendants call your name at the kispum for generations.
You lived as Siduri said, and those whose hands you held remembered you all their lives.

Mesopotamians often buried the dead beneath the house floor or in cemeteries outside the city, with pots, food and ornaments; infants were often buried in clay jars. The land of the dead was thought dark and full of dust, so the dead needed their descendants to offer water and food and call their names at the kispum.
Bury them under the house floor, with a jar of beer and bread
The family lives above them every day, and never forgets to fill the clay pipe with water.
Call their name each month at the kispum
Their name is called for years, as if they still sat in the house.
Hire lamenters to sing for them
The laments carry through the quarter; everyone knows the dead was loved.
The whole city mourns. You are buried in the royal tombs with gold and cosmetic shells.
You are buried in the cemetery outside Ur’s walls, with lapis jewellery and cosmetic shells.
You are buried in a plain grave outside the city. Those who loved you say your name softly as they fill it in.
Your family buries you beneath the house floor with a jar of beer, bread and the pots you used every day.
Those who reach 50 in a Mesopotamian city have much to tell. How would they want their name remembered?

Old Babylonian letters almost all begin this way: “To…, say: thus says…”, because letters were read aloud to the recipient.

An approximate spelling in the style of Sumerian receipts; kaš means beer.
A receipt with your name
An approximate spelling following the receipt formula of the Third Dynasty of Ur; šu ba-an-ti means “received”. Tens of thousands of receipts like this survive.
The river falls so low that no water reaches the canals, and the barley withers in the fields.
The river breaks the levees at night and floods the low quarter; everyone carries the children onto the roofs.

By tradition Memphis was founded by King Menes about 3100 BCE where the valley meets the Delta. It was the capital through the Old Kingdom. Its cemetery at Saqqara holds King Djoser’s Step Pyramid, the world’s first large stone building.

The three pyramids at Giza were built for Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure about 2600–2500 BCE. Archaeologists have found the workers’ town nearby, with bakeries, breweries and masses of cattle bones, and the workers’ own cemetery. The builders were organised, fed crews, not slaves as was once believed.

Egypt’s first kings were buried at Abydos, which later became the centre of the cult of Osiris. Pilgrims left offering pots by the million; local people today call the site Umm el-Qa’ab, “mother of pots”.

Thebes (Waset) was the city of Amun, with the temple of Karnak, added to for nearly two thousand years. Across the river lay the city of the dead, including the Valley of the Kings in the New Kingdom.

Deir el-Medina was the village of the men who cut and decorated the royal tombs in the New Kingdom, with about seventy houses inside its wall. Thousands of inscribed flakes of stone and pottery were found in one great pit, recording laundry lists, debts, quarrels and love songs. Far more of its men could read than elsewhere.

The Fayum is a lake basin west of the Nile. Middle Kingdom kings drained it and opened new fields. The town of Shedet worshipped the crocodile god Sobek, and nearby Lahun left many papyri, including the oldest known medical text about women’s health.

Elephantine is an island at the First Cataract, on the border with Nubia. Its old name, Abu, means “elephant”, perhaps from the ivory trade. It had a Nilometer, used to measure the flood, predict the harvest and set taxes.

Akhenaten built Akhetaten (Amarna) as a new capital for the Aten about 1346 BCE; it was abandoned less than twenty years later. Skeletons of ordinary people from its South Tombs cemetery show heavy labour, and many died young.
The Delta was a vast wetland of papyrus, cattle pastures, hippos and crocodiles. Far less evidence survives from here than from the south, because wet ground destroys papyrus and mud brick.

In Egypt most people farmed land belonging to a temple, the king or a noble. Craftsmen and specialists were paid in bread, beer and grain, and children usually followed their parents’ trade. A Middle Kingdom text, the Satire of the Trades, mocks every job except the scribe’s.

Egyptian society was layered, from king, officials, priests and scribes to craftsmen, farmers and servants. Slavery existed, especially war captives in the New Kingdom, but most labourers were not slaves. Egyptian women could own property, go to court and divorce, which was rare in the ancient world.
The Nile rises too little this year. The water never reaches the higher fields, and the grain must be eked out.
The Nile rises too high this year. It breaks the dykes and washes away several mud-brick houses in the village.
The Nile rises just right and leaves black mud over the fields. It will be a fine harvest.

Every year, around July, the Nile flooded with rain from Ethiopia and left black silt on the fields. Egyptians called their land Kemet, “the black land”. Too low a flood meant famine; too high destroyed villages. The state measured the river with Nilometers to predict the harvest and set taxes. The Aswan High Dam, finished in 1970, ended the flood.
Wrote on papyrus with your own hand
A scribe of the estate writes your name in the list of workers. You cannot read it, but that is your name.
Egyptians believed the name (ren) was part of the self: while your name was spoken, you lived on. Erasing someone’s name from a monument was like killing them a second time.
Your name was written on papyrus
You pay the debt in full, and the creditor scratches your name off the potsherd where he noted it.
Your creditor takes you before the village court. You must swear by the king’s name to pay, and the court seizes goods from your house.

Egypt’s local courts, the kenbet, were made up of villagers and officials. Breaking an oath sworn by the king’s name could bring harsh punishment. Records from Deir el-Medina show some small debt cases dragging on for years.
Taken to court over a debt
Word comes that a king from the south has conquered the Delta and wears the crowns of both lands.
The Narmer Palette, about 3100 BCE, shows a king of Upper Egypt striking an enemy. It is often read as the unification of Egypt, though the real process probably took generations.
At Saqqara a stepped mountain of stone rises over the king’s tomb. People say it was designed by Imhotep, his chief official.
King Djoser’s Step Pyramid, about 2670 BCE, is the first large stone building known. Imhotep was later worshipped as a god of medicine and wisdom.
Each year the king’s pyramid at Giza grows taller. Crews from every village take turns hauling the stone.

Khufu’s Great Pyramid, about 146 metres tall, was the tallest structure on Earth for some 3,800 years. The logbook of a team leader named Merer, written about 2560 BCE, records shipping limestone to Giza; it is the oldest inscribed papyrus known.
For years in a row the Nile rises too little. Many towns’ granaries stand empty, and people walk far in search of grain.

The tomb of Ankhtifi, a local ruler about 2100 BCE, boasts that he fed the hungry while “all of Upper Egypt was dying of hunger”. Many link this time to the worldwide drought of about 4,200 years ago, though this is debated.
The army of King Mentuhotep of Thebes unites the land once more.
Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt about 2055 BCE, beginning the Middle Kingdom.
The king sends workers to dig canals and drain the lake. New fields rise out of the marsh.
Middle Kingdom kings, above all Amenemhat III, greatly developed the Fayum. His mortuary temple at Hawara was called “the Labyrinth” by Greek writers.
Ships return from distant Punt with whole incense trees growing in baskets, baboons and leopard skins. The whole city comes out to watch.

Queen Hatshepsut (reigned about 1479–1458 BCE) sent an expedition to Punt, carved on her temple at Deir el-Bahari. Punt was probably on the southern Red Sea or the Horn of Africa; isotopes in mummified baboons have helped locate it.
Word spreads that the king hunted wild bulls in the desert and killed 96 of them in one hunt.
A commemorative scarab of Amenhotep III records this hunt. The wild bulls were aurochs, the ancestors of cattle; the species died out when the last one died in Poland in 1627.
The king proclaims that only one god should be worshipped: the Aten, the sun disc. Workmen go out to chisel the name of Amun off the temple walls.

Akhenaten (reigned about 1353–1336 BCE) raised the Aten above all other gods. After his death it was all reversed and his name left out of the king lists. Yet in ordinary houses at Amarna archaeologists still found figures of Bes and Taweret.
Word comes that the young king has died, not yet twenty years old.
Tutankhamun died about 1323 BCE; DNA studies found malaria in his mummy. His tomb, found by Howard Carter in 1922, is the best-preserved tomb in the Valley of the Kings, though he was a minor king.
Returning soldiers say the king’s army was nearly routed at Kadesh, yet the temple walls proclaim a mighty victory.
At Kadesh in 1274 BCE Ramesses II fought the Hittites; both sides claimed victory. About sixteen years later they made a peace treaty, one of the oldest whose text survives.
Word comes that a fleet of strangers from the sea has attacked the river mouths, and the king’s army goes to meet them.
Reliefs at Ramesses III’s temple of Medinet Habu show battles with the “Sea Peoples” about 1177 BCE. Many kingdoms around the Mediterranean collapsed at this time; Egypt survived, weakened.
You help load sacks of grain onto the boats and earn bread and beer worth about a deben.

Egypt had no coins. People swapped goods, but reckoned value in deben, a weight of copper (about 91 grams in the New Kingdom), or in sacks of grain. A record of buying an ox might list linen, oil and a basket that together made up the price.
