Egyptians wrote letters and accounts on papyrus, made from strips of the papyrus reed laid crosswise and beaten into a sheet. Papyrus was costly, so short everyday notes were often written on flakes of limestone or broken pottery instead. People who could not read hired a scribe.
You must read and write, or have a deben’s worth of goods to hire a scribe
The flood season: the king’s work
The fields lie under water and no one can farm for months. The king’s officials come to call people from every village to haul stone for the pyramid at Giza.
The fields lie under water and no one can farm for months. Officials come to call people from every village to work for the king, digging canals and building temples.

In the flood season (Akhet), roughly July to October, the fields were under water and the state called up labour for building. Work gangs at Giza had names like “Friends of Khufu” and “Drunkards of Menkaure”, written on the stones. A Middle Kingdom papyrus lists people who fled their labour duty, and family members held until they returned.
Go and work with your village gang
A block slips onto your foot. Your gang carries you to the physician, who binds it with linen and honey.
The work blisters your hands, but there is bread, beer and some days even beef. You come home with friends from many villages.
Send the official a gift so someone else goes
The official takes the gift and crosses out your name. Someone else goes in your place.
Needs 2 deben in goods
Run away to hide in the papyrus marshes
You are tracked down; meanwhile your family has been held in your place.
You hide with the mosquitoes in the marsh until the water falls. No one comes after you.

Most Egyptian names had meanings and often named a god: Amenhotep means “Amun is satisfied”. The hieroglyphs of your name in this game are an approximate spelling. In real writing the god’s name was usually written first, out of respect, even when it was spoken last.
Your mother shows you the god on the temple wall and tells you stories until dark.
Eyes in the shallows
You go with your mother to fetch water and see two eyes and a long snout above the shallows, a few steps away.

Nile crocodiles grow to about 5 metres and killed many people at the river. Egyptians wore amulets and recited spells against them; tomb scenes show herdsmen pointing a finger at the water and chanting as their cattle cross a channel. Today crocodiles live in Egypt only above the Aswan Dam.
Back away slowly
The eyes sink without a ripple. Your mother pulls you back and does not let go of your hand all day.
Throw a stone at it
The crocodile surges out of the water. You fall and scrape your knees running, but you get away.
The crocodile slides into deep water. The other children stare at you in awe.
Shout to warn the other children
The children scramble up the bank. One of their mothers gives you a honey cake.
A hippo in the field
In the middle of the night a huge hippopotamus climbs out of the river into your family’s field and starts eating the young wheat.

Hippos come ashore at night to graze and could wreck a field. A New Kingdom school text describes the farmer’s misery: “the worm has taken half the grain, the hippopotamus has eaten the rest”. Hippos are still among the most dangerous large animals in Africa. In Egypt the last ones were killed in the early 1800s.
Bang pots with your father to drive it off
The hippo bellows and lumbers back into the river. Half the plot is saved.
The hippo turns and charges. Your father pulls you aside just in time, but you twist your ankle.
Hide in the house
By morning the plot is nothing but huge round footprints and mud.
Light torches around the field
The hippo does not like the fire. It stares a long while, then slips back into the water. Your father lights torches every night after that.
The birth bricks
Your mother is about to give birth. The women of the house set out two birth bricks for her to squat on, and hang a little hippo-goddess amulet over the bed.

The goddess Taweret was a pregnant hippo with lion’s paws and a crocodile’s tail, who protected mothers and babies, as did the dwarf god Bes. Egyptian women gave birth squatting on bricks; a painted Middle Kingdom birth brick was found at Abydos. Childbirth was a major cause of death for women.
Hold your mother’s hand
Your mother squeezes your hand until it hurts, and then the baby cries.
Draw Taweret on the wall
Your hippo looks like a fat cow, but all the women say the goddess will surely like it.
Run for the midwife
You run faster than ever in your life, and the midwife arrives just in time.
First day at the scribal school
The teacher has you dip a reed pen in ink and copy signs onto a plastered wooden board, over and over. He says, “A boy’s ear is on his back: he listens when he is beaten.”

Scribal pupils practised on limestone flakes, potsherds and plastered boards, because papyrus was costly. Hieroglyphs were for monuments; for daily writing scribes used a faster cursive, hieratic. The saying about the boy’s ear comes from a New Kingdom school text.
Copy every sign with care
Secretly draw a cat in the margin
No one sees. In the evening the board is whitewashed for reuse, and your cat vanishes with the writing.
The teacher says some pictures stand for sounds: the owl is “m”. You spend the evening staring at the owls on the roof.
The Satire of the Trades

The teacher reads aloud: “I have seen the coppersmith at the mouth of his furnace; his fingers are like crocodile skin, and he stinks worse than fish roe.” It ends: “Be a scribe, and you will be spared hard labour.”

The Satire of the Trades, or Teaching of Khety, is a Middle Kingdom text that scribal pupils copied for a thousand years. It mocks every job, from smith and farmer to washerman, to make pupils study hard. The quotation is paraphrased.
Laugh along with the others
The whole class laughs until the teacher bangs the table.
Think of your father, who farms
That night you look a long time at your father’s hands, and copy harder than ever.
Learn the whole text by heart
You learn it all, and quote it at your friends whenever they complain.
The senet board
Your grandfather brings out a board of thirty squares, throws four flat sticks, and teaches you to move the pieces along the squares.
Senet is one of the oldest board games, found in burials from about 3000 BCE; Tutankhamun’s tomb held several boards. By the New Kingdom it was seen as the soul’s journey through the afterlife.
Play to win
You win. Your grandfather laughs and demands another game.
Your grandfather wins every game, but teaches you one trick.
Let your grandfather win
He knows, but pretends not to, and smiles all evening.
Ask what the last square means
He says it is the way to the Field of Reeds of Osiris, where the wheat grows taller than a man.
Driving the cattle across the channel
You must drive the cattle across a channel to the pasture on the other side. The water is chest-deep, and yesterday someone saw a crocodile here.

Old Kingdom tomb scenes, such as in the tomb of Ti at Saqqara, show a herdsman carrying a calf through the water while it looks back at its mother, and another pointing at a crocodile below and chanting a spell.
Point at the water and chant the spell like the old herdsmen
Every animal crosses safely. You begin to believe the spell works.
The water boils in mid-channel, and a calf is dragged under before your eyes.
Carry the calf on your shoulders
The calf bawls for its mother all the way; she swims close behind, and the whole herd follows.
Wait until the crocodile moves on
You wait until afternoon, see it basking far off, and hurry across.
The hippo hunt in the marsh
The lord of the estate goes hunting hippos from a papyrus skiff, and you are chosen to go along, holding a harpoon on a long rope.

Nobles’ tomb scenes often show the owner harpooning a hippo from a reed boat. The hippo stood for the god Seth and chaos, so killing it echoed Horus defeating disorder. Real hunts were very dangerous: a hippo could easily overturn a boat and kill a man.
Throw the harpoon yourself
Hunted a hippo in the papyrus marsh
The harpoon strikes. The hippo drags the boat until everyone hauls the rope together, and the lord claps your shoulder in front of them all.
The hippo overturns the boat. You nearly drown, and its tusk gashes your leg.
Hold the rope at the stern
The rope cuts your palms bloody, but the boat stays upright.
Ask to stay behind
The lord raises an eyebrow and picks someone else.
Founding a house
Your family and another are talking of you two living together. In Egypt there is no temple ceremony: moving into one house is “founding a house”.

Marriage in Egypt was a family matter, not a religious rite. Later, marriage contracts protected the wife’s property; wives could divorce, and in the New Kingdom often kept about a third of the joint property. In love poems lovers call each other “brother” and “sister”.
Move in together
Founded a house with someone you love
A small room with a bread oven and a reed mat is now your house.
First, compose a love song
You sing that your heart leaps when you think of them. The whole village teases you for months, but the answer is yes.
Your song makes everyone laugh, except the one you sang it to.
The families grumble, but agree to wait.
A letter home
You must work at a distant estate for months. Word comes that the household is quarrelling over grain rations, and someone is bullying the newest member of the family.

The Heqanakht letters, about 1950 BCE, were written home by a farmer-priest. They say exactly how much grain each person should get, and scold the household for mistreating his new wife. Found in a tomb at Thebes, they may never have been delivered. Agatha Christie based her mystery Death Comes as the End on them.
Write a letter setting out every ration
You write out who gets how many sacks, ending: “Let no one mistreat her again.”
You hire a scribe to write it, and have him read it back three times.
Ask for leave to go home
It takes five days to get home and costs you wages, but the house calms down.
Let them sort it out
When you return, nobody has spoken to anybody for months.
Asked for a loan of grain
At Deir el-Medina villagers noted debts on flakes of stone and potsherds, sometimes saying who borrowed what, its value in deben, and who witnessed it.
Lend it, and note it before witnesses
You write the borrower’s name, two sacks of grain and two witnesses on a potsherd.
You have a scribe note it down, with two witnesses.
Write a demand letter on papyrus
Take it to the village court, with your witnesses
You need a written note and witnesses
Asking the god
Your best piece of linen has gone missing, and you suspect a neighbour. Today the priests carry the statue of the deified King Amenhotep I through the village; anyone may put a question to it.

In the New Kingdom people put questions to a god’s statue carried in procession on a model boat. It “answered” by lurching forward or back. At Deir el-Medina villagers asked the deified Amenhotep I, the village’s founder, about everything from thefts to who owned a house.
Ask whether your neighbour took it
The statue lurches forward. Your neighbour turns pale and returns the linen that night, but never greets you again.
The statue moves back: your neighbour did not take it. You must go and apologise.
Read out every household and let the god choose
The statue halts at a house no one expected, and the child there confesses in tears.
Ask nothing, and let it go
You weave a new cloth, and no one is shamed.
“We are hungry!”
The royal tomb-workers’ grain rations are eighteen days late. The whole village’s craftsmen down tools, march out to sit behind the temple, and shout, “We are hungry!”

The Turin Strike Papyrus records that in year 29 of Ramesses III, about 1157 BCE, the royal tomb-workers stopped work because their rations had not come. It is often called the first recorded strike. The scribe Amennakht wrote it down, and in the end the workers got their grain.
Sit down and protest with everyone
Joined the first recorded strike in history
You sit in the sun all day and shout yourself hoarse. Three days later the grain arrives.
Keep working
The foreman praises you, but your neighbours do not greet you for months.
Write a petition to the vizier
Your petition speaks of hunger, and of Ma’at, the right order the king must keep. The vizier sends part of the grain at once.
Gold from a royal tomb
A stonemason whispers that he and his gang broke into an old king’s tomb and took a sack of gold. If you help sell it, you get a share.

Papyri record investigations under Ramesses IX, about 1110 BCE, including the confession of a stonemason named Amenpanefer, who told how his gang broke into the tomb of King Sobekemsaf II and his queen and divided the gold. Tomb robbers faced death by impalement.
Refuse, and say nothing
You sleep badly for many nights, but keep silent.
Report it to the officials
The gang is arrested. You must testify, and several houses in the village look at you coldly.
Help sell it for a share
You are caught with the gang, beaten on the soles of your feet and stripped of everything. Your family is shamed before the whole village.
The gold buys plenty of grain, cloth and cattle, but you flinch whenever an official walks by.
The gods in the house
Officials proclaim that only the Aten may be worshipped. But in your room stand little figures of Bes and Taweret, who have always protected the children of the house.
Archaeologists found figures of Bes, Taweret and amulets of other gods in ordinary houses at Amarna, showing that people kept worshipping the old gods at home, even in the Aten’s own city.
Hide them under the mat
Every night you still whisper to Bes before you sleep.
Smash them as ordered
Your child cries at the broken pieces, and no one in the house sleeps that night.
Worship both the Aten and the house gods
At dawn you raise your hands to the sun; at dusk you leave a cake for Bes. No one knows what you really believe.
Going to the physician
You are ill enough to go to the physician. He examines you, notes something on papyrus, and asks whether you want medicine or a spell.

Egyptian doctors were famous across the ancient world. The Edwin Smith Papyrus, copied about 1600 BCE, describes 48 injuries from head to spine and says whether each should be treated. Physicians dressed wounds with honey, which kills bacteria. Egyptians used medicine and spells together and saw no conflict between them.
Medicine: honey and linen
The physician spreads honey, binds it in clean linen, and tells you to come back in three days.
A spell and an amulet
He chants a spell calling on Isis, and ties an Eye of Horus amulet to your wrist.
Both
Honey for the wound, a spell for the heart. You feel better before you are out of the door.
Needs 1 deben in goods
A painted coffin
The village carpenter makes beautiful painted wooden coffins. One costs as much as many months of a workman’s pay, and your family must decide whether to save for one.

Records from Deir el-Medina show coffins and tomb goods took a large share of a family’s income. Many reused old coffins, scraping off the old name and writing a new one. For Egyptians, preparing for death was not morbid but an investment in eternity.
Save for the coffin
Bought a painted coffin for eternity
The craftsman writes your name on it in black ink. You visit it every month.
Needs 3 deben in goods
Spend it on the children’s schooling instead
One of your children goes to study with a scribe. One day they may write your name.
A pit in the sand is enough
You say the hot sand will keep your body, as it kept the ancestors.
A Book of the Dead
The temple scribes’ workshop sells papyrus scrolls of spells for the afterlife, with painted pictures and blank spaces left for the buyer’s name.

Many Books of the Dead were written in advance, with the dead person’s name added in blank spaces later; in some the blanks were never filled. Spell 125 holds the “declaration of innocence”, such as “I have not stolen… I have not moved the boundary stone…”, which the dead recited before the gods before their heart was weighed.
Buy a long scroll with paintings
Owned a Book of the Dead with your name in it
The scribe fills your name into every blank, and you have him read it to you line by line.
Copy one yourself, spell by spell
It takes months and your hand aches, but every line is in your own writing.
You must read and write well
Too expensive
You recite the short spell your mother taught you instead.
The Festival of Drunkenness
Tonight is Hathor’s festival. Everyone drinks until they are drunk, to remember how red beer once calmed the lioness goddess.

In the myth of the Destruction of Mankind, Ra sends the lioness Sekhmet to punish humans, then stops her with beer dyed red like blood. She drinks herself drunk and becomes gentle Hathor. Evidence from the temple of Mut at Thebes shows that real rites of drunkenness were held in the New Kingdom.
Drink until you see the goddess
You wake at dawn on the temple steps, unsure whether you saw the goddess or dreamed her.
Drink a little and watch the children
You are the only one who remembers what happened, and you tell everyone for days.
Brew red beer for the goddess
You mix red ochre into the beer, and the priests offer your jar first.
The empty granaries
The Nile was low and many granaries are already empty. A neighbour comes begging grain for their children, and the local lord announces he will hand out grain from his stores.
Many Egyptian officials wrote in their tombs, “I gave bread to the hungry and clothes to the naked.” Feeding people in famine proved that a ruler upheld Ma’at, the right order of the world.
Share your grain with the neighbour
The neighbour’s children survive the season. They never forget.
Guard your own store
Your family eats, but every night you hear children crying next door.
Queue for the lord’s grain
The queue starts before dawn, but you bring home a basket of grain.
A letter to the dead

Egyptians wrote “letters to the dead” on bowls or papyrus, asking dead relatives for protection, or to stop troubling the living. One New Kingdom letter is from a man to his dead wife, asking what he did wrong, when he always cared for her.
Ask them to protect the children
Ask forgiveness for what was left unsaid
You write what you never said while they lived, and weep until the bowl is wet.
Simply go and tell them the family news
You sit by the tomb telling them about the grandchild just learning to walk, as if they were still listening.
Servants for the next world
The village potter sells little shabti figures. They say that in the afterlife, when you are called to work the god’s fields, a shabti will answer “Here I am!” and work in your place.

Shabtis were buried with the dead, often inscribed with Spell 6 of the Book of the Dead. By the late New Kingdom some burials had sets of 401: 365 workers, one for each day of the year, and 36 overseers.
Buy a whole set
The shabtis fill the box in rows. You laugh that at last you will never have to farm again.
Just one will do
You choose the one with the most hard-working face.
Make your own, and let the grandchildren paint it
Your shabti’s face is crooked, but the grandchildren paint it a smile.
Teachings for the children
Your children gather round, wanting to hear what life has taught you.

The Teaching of Ptahhotep, attributed to an Old Kingdom vizier and preserved in Middle Kingdom copies, is one of the world’s oldest books of advice. It says: “Do not be proud of your knowledge; consult the ignorant as well as the wise.”
Write your teaching down
You write: “Listen to those who cannot read as well, for they know what books do not.”
Tell them by the oven
The youngest grandchild falls asleep in your lap before you finish.
Tell them all to become scribes
Everyone laughs: you sound exactly like a schoolteacher.
The Beautiful Festival of the Valley
Amun’s boat crosses to the west bank. Every family carries food and flowers to their ancestors’ tombs, to eat, drink and spend the night with the dead.

The Beautiful Festival of the Valley was held every year at Thebes in the New Kingdom, a day when the living and the dead “dined together”. Tomb paintings show banquets with musicians, lotus flowers and wine.
Tell the grandchildren about the ancestors
You talk late into the night, and the old names are spoken again and again under the lamp.
Sit quietly by a loved one’s tomb
The desert wind cools, and you feel someone sitting beside you.
The cattle count
You go with an official to count cattle and collect taxes in the villages. One village head is short, and the overseers stand behind him with sticks.

Old Kingdom tomb scenes show scribes writing numbers while village heads who fell short on taxes are dragged forward and beaten. The national cattle count was so important that years were named after it, as in “the year of the tenth count”.
Record every animal truly
Your figures are exact. The official is pleased, but you cannot meet the village head’s eyes.
Skip two scrawny cows in the count
The official recounts them himself, and stares at you for a long time.
The village head is spared the stick. He sends you dried fish every year after.
The stone crew’s logbook
The team leader has you keep a daily log: how many boatloads of limestone the crew carries from the Tura quarries to Giza, where they stop, and what they eat.

In 2013 archaeologists found papyri at the harbour of Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea: the logbook of a team leader named Merer, under King Khufu, describing how his crew shipped limestone for the Great Pyramid. They are the oldest inscribed papyri known.
Note everything in detail
Your log fills several rolls. The leader keeps it in a wooden box.
Write your own name at the end of the roll
Wrote your own name into the pyramid builders’ log
Your name may outlast even the pyramid’s smooth casing.
The vanished boundary stone
The flood has gone down and mud has buried the field markers. You see your neighbour quietly setting a new stone two paces into your land.

After each flood, state “rope-stretchers” re-measured the fields. The Teaching of Amenemope warns, “Do not move the markers on the borders of fields”, and in Spell 125 the dead must declare before the gods, “I have not moved the boundary stone.”
Call the rope-stretchers to measure again
The taut rope proves you right, and the stone goes back.
Move it back yourself at night
Next morning your neighbour looks at the stone, then at you, and says nothing.
Push your own marker into their field
Your field grows a little, but whenever you hear Spell 125 you feel cold.
A hippo under the skiff
As you spread your nets in the marsh, the water bulges under your papyrus skiff. A hippo is about to surface right beneath you.
Egyptian fishermen used skiffs of bundled papyrus, light and easy to overturn. Tomb scenes show them with drag nets and throwing sticks for birds, while hippos and crocodiles lurk under the water.
Jump and swim for the bank
You make for the reeds, but a crocodile snaps at your leg before your friend hauls you out.
You reach the bank, too breathless to speak. Your skiff floats upside down in the marsh.
Lie flat and still in the boat
The hippo surfaces beside the boat, snorts, and sinks away elsewhere.
The boat flips. You come up tangled in your own nets.
Slap the water with your pole as loud as you can
The noise turns the hippo away, and every bird in the marsh rises at once.
Beer from malt
The head brewer does it the old way, baking beer bread and crumbling it into water. A young brewer says that if you sprout the grain and cook part of it, the beer comes out sweeter.

Microscope studies of residues in beer jars from Deir el-Medina and Amarna, by the archaeologist Delwen Samuel in the 1990s, showed that brewers mixed cooked and uncooked malted grain. Egyptian beer was thick and sweetish, and workers’ daily rations often included bread and several jugs of beer.
Try the new way
The beer is so sweet the workers queue for it. The head brewer grumbles, then quietly asks for the method.
The first batch turns sour, but you learn how long to cook it.
Keep to the old way
Your beer tastes like your grandfather’s, and that is no bad thing.
Khnum’s wheel
Your master says the god Khnum shapes every child on his potter’s wheel before placing it in its mother’s womb, so a potter must make every pot as carefully as the god.

Egyptians believed the ram-headed Khnum shaped people’s bodies and their ka on a potter’s wheel; temple reliefs show him modelling the infant king. The potter’s wheel was used in Egypt from the Old Kingdom.
Throw slowly, one pot at a time
Your pots grow so thin and light that the priests order them for the temple.
Throw fast, and make many
The yard fills with pots, and you trade for more grain than ever.
Hauling the sledge
Your gang must drag a huge block on a wooden sledge across the sand. The ropes strain to breaking. An old hand tells you to pour water on the sand in front of the sledge.

A Middle Kingdom painting in the tomb of Djehutihotep shows a man pouring water in front of a sledge carrying a colossal statue. A 2014 experiment found that sand wetted just right roughly halves the force needed to pull.
Pour the water as the old hand says
The sledge slides forward as if someone were pushing, and the gang cheers.
Just pull harder
The block creeps along; everyone’s hands are bleeding before sunset.
Sing a rhythm for the gang
Everyone pulls together to your song, and the other gangs start singing it too.
A day off to brew beer
Tomorrow is a family feast and you want a day off from the royal tomb to brew beer. The gang’s scribe notes everyone who is absent, and why.

Ostraca from Deir el-Medina record why workmen were absent: brewing beer, being stung by a scorpion, embalming a relative, a wife or daughter menstruating, even “offering to his god”. Workers were issued counted lamp wicks, which also measured their hours in the dark.
Take the day and brew
Beside your name the scribe writes, “absent: brewing beer”. Three thousand years later someone may read it and laugh.
Keep working by lamplight
You finish painting Anubis on the tomb wall, and the master craftsman nods.
Seventy days
A poor family brings their mother’s body to be embalmed, but can only pay for the cheapest treatment. Your master says to do only what they paid for.

The Greek writer Herodotus describes three price grades of embalming. The best removed the brain through the nose with an iron hook, took out the organs and dried the body in natron salt; the whole process took seventy days. The heart was left in the body, to be weighed in the afterlife.
Do your best work anyway
You use your own natron and linen. The dead woman’s daughter kisses your hand when she comes for the body.
Do only what they paid for
The work is quick, your master is pleased, and the family never knows there was better.
Slip in an amulet at no charge
You lay a scarab amulet over her heart, so the heart will say nothing against her at the weighing.
Carrying the god’s boat
You are one of the priests carrying the god’s sacred boat in procession. A poor farmer asks the god whether a field is his or a rich man’s, and the rich man catches your eye.
In an oracle, the answer came from how the boat, carried by many priests, moved, so it could be swayed. Some records show losers taking their question to another god.
Let the god decide
The boat leans towards the farmer, who weeps. You will never know whose arms moved it.
Lean your shoulder toward the rich man
The boat leans to the rich man. Next day a sack of grain appears at your door, and you lie awake for nights.
The broken skull
Workmen carry in a man hit on the head by a falling stone. His skull is broken and he cannot speak. Your book says: “an ailment not to be treated.”

The Edwin Smith Papyrus sorts injuries into “an ailment I will treat”, “an ailment I will contend with” and “an ailment not to be treated”. It contains the oldest known description of the brain, and notes that a head injury can weaken or paralyse the limbs.
Treat him as best you can
He wakes on the third day and slowly says his children’s names. You write the case down for your pupils.
He dies that night. His family does not blame you, but you blame yourself.
Follow the book and let him rest in peace
You sit beside him chanting a spell for easy sleep until he slips away.
The overseer of women physicians
You hear that at the palace there is a woman with the title “overseer of women physicians”. People in the village say women should only be midwives.
An Old Kingdom tomb inscription of a woman named Peseshet, about 2500 BCE, gives her the title “overseer of women physicians”. She is one of the earliest women in medicine known by name.
Travel to learn from her
She sets you to tend the palace women, and teaches you remedies no man has read.
Keep treating your village
Soon the people who said women cannot be physicians bring you their sick children.
The fortress at the cataract
Your company is posted to a mud-brick fortress at the Second Cataract in Nubia, checking every boat and caravan on the river.

Middle Kingdom kings built great fortresses along the Second Cataract, such as Buhen, with thick walls and ditches. Military dispatches from them record even small groups of Nubians passing. The forts now lie under Lake Nasser, drowned by the Aswan High Dam.
Search every boat thoroughly
You catch a man smuggling ivory, and your commander sends a report to the king.
Make friends with the Nubian traders
One trader teaches you words of his language and gives you an ostrich feather.
The enemy chariots
The army marches far to the north. Suddenly hundreds of enemy chariots burst from behind a hill and cut the column in two.
Horse-drawn chariots came into Egypt shortly before the New Kingdom and became the core of the imperial army. At Kadesh in 1274 BCE, Hittite chariots ambushed Ramesses II’s army and nearly routed it.
Hold the shield line
Your line holds, and the chariots wheel away.
The horses crash into the line, and you are trampled, ribs broken.
Run for the camp
You survive, but on the march home no one tells the story with you in it.

In Egypt the wind usually blows from the north while the river flows north, so boats sailed south and drifted north. The hieroglyph for “travel south” is a boat with its sail up; “travel north” is a boat with its sail down.
You swim with your friends in the irrigation canal while your mother shouts from the bank to watch for crocodiles.
Your mother shaves your head, leaving one long lock beside your ear, like every child in the village.
Egyptian children’s heads were often shaved except for a “sidelock of youth”, which helped against lice and heat. The lock became the sign of childhood in Egyptian art.
The house cat drops a small snake at the door and sits waiting for praise.
House cats descend from the African wildcat and lived with Egyptians from early times, catching mice in the granaries and snakes in the house. Later they became sacred to the goddess Bastet.
Your father carves you a little wooden lion whose jaw snaps when you pull a string.
Wooden toy animals with string-worked jaws survive from New Kingdom Egypt; one is in the British Museum.
The children play tug-of-war in the village square, and your side tumbles over in a heap.
Old Kingdom tomb scenes show children playing tug-of-war, leaping games and spinning games, with the words they shout written beside them.
Your aunt keeps bees in clay pots, and today you eat bread with honey.
The oldest known carving of beekeeping comes from King Niuserre’s sun temple, about 2400 BCE. Egyptians used honey both as food and as a dressing for wounds.
A crocodile drags one of your goats into the river as it bends to drink.
A woman washing linen at the end of the village is dragged into the river by a crocodile. The whole village mourns.
A hippo overturns a fishing boat in mid-river, and two of the men aboard drown.
A scorpion hiding in your sandal stings your foot, which swells and throbs for days.
Scorpions were an everyday danger. Priests of the goddess Serqet acted as healers of scorpion and snake bites, with both remedies and spells.
Your eyes are red and sore from dust and flies. Your mother rims them with black kohl.
Egyptian men and women lined their eyes with black kohl made from galena, a lead ore, or green malachite. A 2010 study suggested lead compounds in kohl may have helped the body fight eye infections.
You bite into bread and crunch on grit. A back tooth has throbbed for weeks.
Most Egyptian mummies and skeletons show heavily worn teeth from the sand, grit and quern dust in their bread. Tooth abscesses were common, even among the elite.
A swarm of locusts comes down like a black cloud and eats the wheat to stubble.
A hot desert wind blows sand for three days. Everyone covers their faces with linen and stays indoors.
Before dawn the star Sopdet rises again after seventy days out of sight. Everyone knows the flood is near, and a new year has begun.

The dawn rising of Sirius (Sopdet) came around the start of the Nile flood. Egyptians used a calendar of 365 days, twelve months of thirty days plus five extra, which is the ancestor of the calendar we use today.
At the Opet festival the sacred boat of Amun is carried from Karnak to Luxor, and the temple hands out bread and beer to everyone.
The Opet festival was held every year at Thebes in the New Kingdom and lasted weeks. A record from the reign of Ramesses III lists more than 11,000 loaves and hundreds of jars of beer handed out.
Pilgrims from all over Egypt come to watch the mysteries of Osiris’s death and rebirth. Many leave stone slabs carved with their own names beside the procession route.
Well-off Egyptians often set up stelae at Abydos so that their names would “take part” in Osiris’s festival forever, even if they were buried elsewhere.
The official Harkhuf returns from Nubia with a dwarf who dances for the gods. The boy king writes that he longs to see him more than all the tribute.
Harkhuf copied the letter of the boy king Pepi II onto his tomb wall at Aswan. The king orders men to guard the dwarf all night so he will not fall into the water. It can still be read today.
The priests read the water level on the Nilometer steps and send word by boat to the towns downstream.
Nubians bring a giraffe as tribute for the king, with a little monkey clinging to its long neck. The children run after the procession all the way.
The tomb of the vizier Rekhmire at Thebes shows Nubians bringing a giraffe, monkeys, leopards and ivory. Giraffes no longer lived in Egypt by then, though prehistoric rock art shows they once did.
At dusk a lion roars from the desert edge, and the herdsmen bring the cattle in early.

Lions still lived along Egypt’s desert edges. A commemorative scarab of Amenhotep III boasts of 102 lions killed in his first ten years. North African lions vanished from the wild in the 20th century.
Hunters come back from the desert with a hartebeest with long curved horns. The nobles keep tame ones in pens to fatten.
Old Kingdom tomb scenes show hartebeest, oryx and gazelles kept in pens like farm animals. The hartebeest of Egypt and North Africa, the bubal hartebeest, became extinct in the early 20th century.
In the reed marsh you see a wild bull as big as a horse, with horns nearly a metre long. It stares at you, then walks off into the reeds.
The aurochs, ancestor of domestic cattle, still lived in Egypt’s marshes and was hunted by kings. The last one in the world died in Poland in 1627.
A big flock of white ibises with black heads stalks the fields for worms after the flood.
The sacred ibis belonged to Thoth, god of writing; in later times millions were mummified. It no longer lives wild in Egypt.
Workers are carving a giant lion with the king’s face out of the bedrock beside the causeway to the pyramid.
The Great Sphinx of Giza, about 73 metres long, was carved from a single outcrop of bedrock, most likely under King Khafre, around 2500 BCE.
In the workers’ town the bakeries run all night, and every few days cattle are slaughtered to feed the crews.
On clear mornings you can see the pyramids gleaming white on the horizon.
The Giza pyramids were once cased in polished white Tura limestone. Most of it was stripped in the Middle Ages to build Cairo; a little survives near the top of Khafre’s pyramid.
The new king is a woman. Her statues wear the false beard of kingship, and the market argues about it endlessly.
Hatshepsut ruled as pharaoh about 1479–1458 BCE. Decades after her death many of her images and names were destroyed, perhaps to tidy the line of succession.
Water-carriers drive their donkeys up from the river every day, for the valley village has no well.
Your neighbour has written a love song on a potsherd and reads it to the whole courtyard until everyone hoots.
The king’s chariot races down the royal road through the city, and people raise their hands to the rays of the Aten.
The king has reigned so long that no one in the village remembers any other.
Pepi II may have reigned for 64 or even 94 years; the number is debated. After his long reign the Old Kingdom declined.
At the feast everyone holds a blue lotus flower to smell, and the scent drifts across the courtyard.
A big boat sails south against the current, while another, its sail lowered, drifts north with the stream.
Your eyes have grown so dim that a grandchild must sort the grain for you.
You sit in the sun outside the house, watching your grandchildren swim in the canal where you once swam.
You read how Sinuhe, an official of the palace, hears of the old king’s death and flees Egypt in terror, nearly dying of thirst in the desert.
You read how Sinuhe lives among the people of Retjenu, marries a chieftain’s daughter and grows rich.
You read how the strongman of Retjenu challenges Sinuhe, who dodges his axe and kills him with a single arrow.
You read how old Sinuhe dreads dying abroad, wrapped in a sheepskin instead of linen, and how the king writes inviting him home and promising him a tomb.
You read how Sinuhe returns to the palace, where the king’s children laugh at his foreign looks, and the king gives him a house and a pyramid tomb.

The Tale of Sinuhe was written in the Middle Kingdom, about 1875 BCE. Egyptians considered it a masterpiece and copied it in school for centuries. At its heart is the longing to die and be buried in one’s own land.
The storyteller tells of a shipwrecked sailor on an island, visited by a giant golden serpent with a beard of lapis lazuli.
The serpent tells the sailor how a falling star burned its whole family, leaving it alone, and sends him home with gifts.
The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor is a Middle Kingdom story, one of the oldest island adventure tales in the world.
The storyteller tells of a magician who threw a wax crocodile into a pool, where it became a real one seven cubits long.

This comes from the Westcar Papyrus, a collection of tales about magicians at King Khufu’s court. Another tells of a magician who folded back the water of a lake to find a pendant a rowing girl had dropped.
Ibises probe the mud along the canal.
A hippo grunts from the dark river.
A crocodile basks open-jawed on a sandbank.
Boats with full sails run south against the current on the north wind.
The smell of baking bread drifts through the village.
A line of donkeys carries sacks of grain to the granary.
Women beat linen against the stones at the canal.
The papyrus reeds rustle in the wind.
The sun sets behind the western desert, the land of the dead.
The village dogs bark at a passing donkey caravan.
The whitewashed house walls glare in the sun.
Date palms sway along the river.
Children chase the geese round the courtyard.
A kingfisher dives for fish in the canal.
The shaduf creaks as it lifts water into the vegetable garden.

The kings who united Egypt will be followed by some thirty dynasties over nearly three thousand years. The signs your generation began to write will be carved on temples until 394 CE, the last known hieroglyphic inscription, on the island of Philae.
The pyramids built in your lifetime will stand for more than 4,500 years. Of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, only the Great Pyramid still stands.
After years of hunger and civil war, a king from Thebes will reunite the land. Later writers looked back on your age as a time of chaos, and wrote laments about it.

Writers of your age created tales and teachings that Egyptians would copy in school for a thousand years. The language of this period is the classical Egyptian that Egyptology students still learn first today.

Egypt’s empire will reach from Nubia to Syria, then shrink. Within a thousand years Persians, Greeks and Romans will rule the Nile. Yet the tombs your age cut into the hills will draw visitors from all over the world.
Then for some fourteen centuries no one could read hieroglyphs, until Jean-François Champollion deciphered them in 1822 with the help of the Rosetta Stone.
The hippos you saw in the river were hunted out of Egypt; the last were killed in the early 1800s.
Nile crocodiles survive in Egypt today only above the Aswan High Dam.
The wild bulls you saw were aurochs; the last in the world died in 1627.
The lions of the desert edge vanished from North Africa in the 20th century.
The hartebeest you saw died out entirely in the early 20th century.
Sacred ibises no longer live wild in Egypt.
Your Book of the Dead, with your name in its blank spaces, was laid in your tomb. Perhaps it is in a museum today, labelled with your name.
On an ostracon listing absences, your name stands beside the words “brewing beer”.
The bowl you wrote to the dead may still be waiting under the sand.
You never wrote, but your name is in someone else’s list. Egyptians believed that whenever someone reads a name aloud, its owner lives again.

Egyptians believed the dead travelled to the Hall of Judgement, where the heart was weighed against the feather of Ma’at. A heart heavy with wrongdoing was eaten by Ammit, with a crocodile’s head, a lion’s body and a hippo’s hindquarters. Those who could afford it were mummified; the poor were buried in pits in the desert sand, whose heat and dryness could preserve a body naturally.
Pay the embalmers
The embalmers work for seventy days. The family weeps again when the linen-wrapped body comes home.
Bury them in the desert sand, with bread and beer
The hot sand will keep the body. The family sets a jar of beer beside the head.
Recite the offering prayer on every feast day
On every feast day you stand at the grave and say: “An offering that the king gives: bread and beer for the ka of the departed.”
You are mummified for seventy days and laid in a tomb cut into the desert cliff, its walls painted with your life, among furniture, food and models of servants.
You are buried in a simple pit at the desert edge, wrapped in a reed mat.
Your family lays you in the painted coffin you saved for, in the family’s shared tomb in the desert.
Your family buries you in a pit in the desert sand with jars of bread and beer and the things you used every day. The hot, dry sand preserves your body.
Those who reach 50 beside the Nile have seen fifty floods. How would they want their name remembered?
